rationale: Sirach identifies Joshua son of Nun as Moses' successor. Numbers records Moses presenting Joshua before Eleazar and the congregation, laying hands on him, and giving him authority so Israel will obey him.
source_text: Mighty in war was Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ successor in prophecies. In keeping with his name he became great in the salvation of His chosen ones, taking vengeance on enemies who rose against them, so that he might give Israel its inheritance.

target_units.text: And the Lord spoke unto Moses, saying: Take unto yourself Joshua son of Nun, a man who has spirit within him, and you shall lay your hands upon him,
and shall set him before Eleazar the priest, and shall instruct him before all the congregation, and shall give instructions concerning him before them,
and shall put of your glory upon him, that the sons of Israel may obey him.

And he shall stand before Eleazar the priest, and they shall ask him for the judgment of the manifestations before the Lord. At his word they shall go out, and at his word they shall come in: he, the sons of Israel together, and the whole congregation.
And Moses did as the Lord commanded him. He took Joshua and stood him before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation.
And he laid his hands on him and presented him, as the Lord had commanded Moses.

rationale: Sirach praises Joshua for giving Israel its inheritance after warfare. Joshua's narrative closes the conquest summary by saying that he gave the land to Israel as tribal inheritances and that the land ceased being at war.
source_text: Mighty in war was Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ successor in prophecies. In keeping with his name he became great in the salvation of His chosen ones, taking vengeance on enemies who rose against them, so that he might give Israel its inheritance.

target_units.text: Joshua took all the land, as the Lord had commanded Moses, and Joshua gave these as an inheritance to Israel, in a division according to their tribes. And the land ceased being at war.

rationale: Sirach recalls Joshua stretching out an armed hand against cities. At Ai, Joshua stretches his hand toward the city and the ambush rises to capture it; the target specifies a javelin, whereas Sirach calls the weapon a sword.
source_text: How glorious he was when he raised his hands and stretched out his sword against cities!

target_units.text: The Lord said to Joshua, “Stretch out your hand with the javelin you hold toward the city, for I have delivered it into your hands. The ambush shall rise quickly from its place.” Joshua stretched out his hand, with the javelin, toward the city,
and the ambush rose quickly from its place. They came out when he stretched out his hand, went to the city, captured it, and hurried to burn it with fire.

rationale: Sirach characterizes Joshua's campaigns as the Lord's wars. Joshua's account of the exceptional day at Gibeon expressly says that the Lord fought alongside Israel.
source_text: Who before him stood so firm? For he himself brought on the Lord’s wars.

target_units.text: There was no such day before or afterward, when God listened to a human being, for the Lord fought alongside Israel.

rationale: Sirach's extended day and restrained sun recall Joshua's request that the sun stand over Gibeon. The narrative says that the sun did not advance toward sunset for a full day and that God listened to Joshua.
source_text: Was not the sun held back by his hand, and did not one day become as two?

target_units.text: Then Joshua spoke to the Lord on the day God handed the Amorites over to Israel, when He crushed them at Gibeon and they were crushed before the sons of Israel. Joshua said, “Let the sun stand over Gibeon, and the moon over the ravine of Aijalon.”
The sun stood, and the moon remained still, until God repelled their enemies. The sun stood in the middle of heaven and did not advance toward sunset for a full day.
There was no such day before or afterward, when God listened to a human being, for the Lord fought alongside Israel.

rationale: Sirach joins Joshua's appeal to the Lord with an answer through hailstones. Joshua's narrative describes the Lord hurling hailstones on the fleeing enemies, records Joshua speaking to the Lord, and concludes that God listened to a human being.
source_text: He called upon the Most High Ruler when enemies pressed him on every side, and the great Lord answered him with hailstones of mighty power.

target_units.text: The Lord threw them into confusion before the sons of Israel, and the Lord crushed them with a great defeat at Gibeon. They pursued them along the ascent of Horonin and cut them down as far as Azekah and Makkedah.

As they fled before the sons of Israel down the descent of Horonin, the Lord hurled hailstones from heaven upon them as far as Azekah. More died from the hailstones than the sons of Israel killed with the sword in battle.

rationale: Sirach places the enemies' destruction on a descent. Joshua locates the rout and heaven-sent hailstones on the descent of Horonin, giving a concrete setting for this recollection of the Lord's warfare.
source_text: He hurled war down upon a nation and destroyed those who resisted on the descent, so that the nations might know his full armament, because his war was before the Lord.

rationale: Sirach names Joshua and Caleb as the two who opposed the assembly's rebellious grumbling. Numbers records them tearing their garments, praising the land, and urging the congregation not to desert the Lord or fear its inhabitants.
source_text: For he followed the Ruler, and in Moses’ days he showed mercy, he and Caleb son of Jephunneh, by standing against the assembly, restraining the people from sin, and stilling wicked grumbling.

target_units.text: And Moses and Aaron fell on their faces before the whole congregation of the sons of Israel.
Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh, among those who had explored the land, tore their garments.
And they said to the whole congregation of the sons of Israel: The land we inspected is exceedingly, exceedingly good.
If the Lord chooses us, He will bring us into this land and give it to us, a land flowing with milk and honey.
Only do not become deserters from the Lord. Do not fear the people of the land, for they are food for us. Their season has passed away from them, but the Lord is among us. Do not fear them.
And the whole congregation said to stone them with stones. Then the Lord’s glory appeared in a cloud over the Tent of Testimony among all the sons of Israel.

rationale: Sirach recalls the exceptional preservation of Joshua and Caleb for entry into the promised land. Numbers excludes the grumbling generation from entry but expressly excepts these two men; their survival is the shared point, without deriving Sirach's troop figure from this passage.
source_text: They alone, being two, were preserved from six hundred thousand foot soldiers, to bring them into an inheritance, into a land flowing with milk and honey.

target_units.text: Say to them, I live, says the Lord: I will certainly do to you just as you have spoken into My ears.
In this wilderness your bodies shall fall, with your entire registration and those of you counted from twenty years old and upward who grumbled against Me.
You shall certainly not enter the land over which I stretched out My hand to settle you upon it, except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun.
And I will bring into the land the children whom you said would become plunder, and they shall inherit the land from which you turned away.

rationale: Sirach says that Joshua and Caleb alone survived from the earlier generation for the inheritance. The later census explicitly reports that none of the men registered in the wilderness remained except Joshua and Caleb.
source_text: They alone, being two, were preserved from six hundred thousand foot soldiers, to bring them into an inheritance, into a land flowing with milk and honey.

target_units.text: And this was the registration by Moses and Eleazar the priest, who registered the sons of Israel in Araboth of Moab beside the Jordan opposite Jericho.
And among these there was no man from those registered by Moses and Aaron, when they registered the sons of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai.
For the Lord had said of them: They shall certainly die in the wilderness. Not one of them remained except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun.

rationale: Sirach praises Caleb's enduring strength, mountain inheritance, and descendants' possession. Caleb says that he is still strong at eighty-five, asks for the mountain, recalls the promise to his children, and receives Hebron.
source_text: The Lord gave Caleb strength, and it remained with him until old age, so that he might mount the high places of the land; his offspring possessed an inheritance,

target_units.text: Moses swore on that day, saying, ‘The land on which you have trodden shall be a lot for you and your children for ever, for you gave yourself to follow the Lord our God.’

Now the Lord has sustained me, as He said. This is the forty-fifth year since the Lord spoke this word to Moses and Israel journeyed in the wilderness. And now, look: today I am eighty-five years old.
I am still strong today, as when Moses sent me; I am just as strong now to go out and come in for war.

Now I ask you for this mountain, as the Lord said on that day, for you heard this word on that day. The Anakim are now there, and great, fortified cities. If the Lord is with me, I shall destroy them, as the Lord said to me.”
Joshua blessed him and gave Hebron to Caleb son of Jephunneh son of Kenaz as a lot.
Therefore Hebron has belonged to Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite as a lot to this day, because he followed the command of the Lord, the God of Israel.

rationale: Sirach's account of Caleb's offspring inheriting land recalls the Lord's promise that Caleb would enter the land and his seed would inherit it because he followed the Lord.
source_text: The Lord gave Caleb strength, and it remained with him until old age, so that he might mount the high places of the land; his offspring possessed an inheritance,

target_units.text: But My servant Caleb, because a different spirit was in him and he followed Me, I will bring into the land he entered, and his seed shall inherit it.

rationale: Sirach draws the lesson that following the Lord is good from Caleb's experience. Joshua explains Caleb's lasting possession of Hebron by his following the command of the Lord, making the same connection between his loyalty and inheritance.
source_text: so that all the sons of Israel might see that it is good to walk after the Lord.

rationale: Sirach honors judges who did not turn from the Lord. Judges describes the Lord raising judges and remaining with them to rescue Israel, while distinguishing the people's recurring abandonment of the Lord after a judge died.
source_text: The judges too, each by his own name, whose hearts did not prostitute themselves and who did not turn away from the Lord—may their remembrance be among blessings!

target_units.text: The Lord raised up judges for them and saved them from the hand of their plunderers.

Yet they did not listen even to their judges, for they prostituted themselves after other gods, bowed down to them, and provoked the Lord. They quickly turned aside from the way their fathers had walked in obeying the Lord’s commandments. They did not do as their fathers had done.

Whenever the Lord raised up judges for them, the Lord was with the judge and saved them from the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge. For the Lord was moved by their groaning before those who besieged and harmed them.

When the judge died, they turned back and again acted more corruptly than their fathers, following other gods to serve them and bow down to them. They did not cast away their practices or depart from their hard way.

rationale: Sirach commemorates faithful judges as a group. Hebrews names Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah among those remembered for faith and victories, offering another retrospective honoring of these leaders.
source_text: The judges too, each by his own name, whose hearts did not prostitute themselves and who did not turn away from the Lord—may their remembrance be among blessings!

target_units.text: And what more shall I say? For time will fail me as I recount Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David and Samuel and the prophets,
who through faith subdued kingdoms, worked righteousness, obtained promises, shut the mouths of lions,
extinguished the power of fire, escaped the edges of the sword, were strengthened from weakness, became mighty in battle, and turned back the armies of foreigners.

rationale: Sirach wishes that the judges' bones would flourish again; Isaiah describes bones springing up like vegetation when the Lord's servants rejoice. The shared image expresses renewed flourishing without requiring both passages to describe the same event.
source_text: May their bones flourish again from their place, and may their name pass onward to their honored sons.

target_units.text: You will see, and your heart will rejoice; your bones will spring up like vegetation. The Lord’s hand will be known to those who revere Him, and He will threaten the disobedient.

rationale: The wish that honored predecessors' bones flourish again from their place recurs nearly word for word. Sirach applies it here to the judges and later to the twelve prophets.
source_text: May their bones flourish again from their place, and may their name pass onward to their honored sons.

target_units.text: May the bones of the twelve prophets flourish again from their place! For they comforted Jacob and redeemed them with the faithfulness of hope.

rationale: Sirach credits Samuel with anointing Israel's rulers. In the narrative whose preceding verses identify Saul, Samuel pours oil on him and declares that the Lord has anointed him ruler over Israel.
source_text: Beloved by his Lord, Samuel, the Lord’s prophet, established a kingdom and anointed rulers over His people.

target_units.text: Samuel took the flask of oil, poured it on his head, kissed him, and said to him, “Has not the Lord anointed you as ruler over His people, over Israel? You will rule among the Lord’s people and save them from their enemies’ hand all around. This will be the sign to you that the Lord has anointed you as ruler over His inheritance:

rationale: Sirach's reference to Samuel anointing rulers also corresponds to David's anointing. The Lord instructs Samuel to anoint David, and Samuel anoints David among his brothers.
source_text: Beloved by his Lord, Samuel, the Lord’s prophet, established a kingdom and anointed rulers over His people.

target_units.text: He sent and brought him. He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes, and good to look upon before the Lord. The Lord said to Samuel, “Rise and anoint David, for this one is good.”
Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him among his brothers. The Lord’s Spirit leaped upon David from that day onward. Samuel rose and went to Armathaim.

rationale: Sirach describes Samuel judging the assembly. The narrative says that he judged Israel throughout his life and lists the circuit of places where he carried out that responsibility.
source_text: By the Lord’s law he judged the assembly, and the Lord visited Jacob.

target_units.text: Samuel judged Israel throughout his life.
Year after year he traveled a circuit through Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, judging Israel in all these consecrated places.
He would return to Armathaim, for his house was there. There he judged Israel, and there he built an altar to the Lord.

rationale: Sirach joins Samuel's prophetic reliability with recognition of his words. The narrative says none of his words fell to the ground and that all Israel recognized him as a faithful prophet to the Lord.
source_text: By his faithfulness he was proved a prophet, and through his words he was known to be trustworthy in vision.

target_units.text: Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him, and none of his words fell to the ground.
All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel was faithful as a prophet to the Lord.

The Lord continued to make Himself known at Shiloh, for the Lord revealed Himself to Samuel. Samuel was recognized as a prophet of the Lord for all Israel, from the ends of the land to the ends. Eli was very old, and his sons continued on their way, and their way was evil before the Lord.

rationale: Sirach recalls Samuel appealing to the Lord amid an enemy threat while offering a suckling lamb. The narrative supplies all three details: the enemy advance, Samuel's prayer for Israel, and the nursing lamb offered as a whole burnt offering.
source_text: He called upon the Lord, the Ruler, when his enemies pressed him on every side, with an offering of a suckling lamb.

target_units.text: The foreigners heard that all the sons of Israel had gathered at Mizpah, and the foreigners’ satraps went up against Israel. When the sons of Israel heard, they were afraid of the foreigners.
The sons of Israel said to Samuel, “Do not be silent on our behalf: keep crying to the Lord your God, and He will save us from the foreigners’ hand.”
Samuel took one nursing lamb and, with all the people, offered it as a whole burnt offering to the Lord. Samuel cried to the Lord for Israel, and the Lord heard him.

rationale: Sirach's heavenly thunder and great divine voice recall the Lord thundering with a great voice against the attacking foreigners while Samuel offered the sacrifice.
source_text: The Lord thundered from heaven and made His voice heard with a great sound.

target_units.text: While Samuel was offering the whole burnt offering, the foreigners drew near for battle against Israel. The Lord thundered with a great voice against the foreigners that day. They were thrown into confusion and fell before Israel.

rationale: Sirach attributes the defeat of hostile rulers to Samuel's period. The narrative describes enemy satraps advancing, their defeat during Samuel's intercession, and the Lord humbling the foreigners throughout Samuel's days; it does not name the Tyrian leaders mentioned by Sirach.
source_text: He destroyed the leaders of the Tyrians and all the rulers of the Philistines.

Israel’s men went out from Mizpah, pursued the foreigners, and struck them as far as below Beth-chor.
Samuel took one stone and set it between Mizpah and the old city. He named it Ebenezer, Stone of the Helper, and said, “Thus far the Lord has helped us.”
The Lord humbled the foreigners, and they did not enter Israel’s territory again. The Lord’s hand was against the foreigners throughout Samuel’s days.

rationale: Sirach recalls Samuel's public declaration that he had taken no property, not even sandals, and the absence of accusations. The narrative preserves his challenge before the Lord and His anointed, explicitly mentions a sandal, and records the people's confirmation that he had taken nothing.
source_text: Before the time of his everlasting sleep, he testified before the Lord and His anointed: “I have taken no property—not even sandals—from any human being.” And no person brought an accusation against him.

target_units.text: Here I am. Answer against me before the Lord and before His anointed: Whose calf have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Which of you have I tyrannized? Whom have I squeezed? From whose hand have I taken an appeasing payment and a sandal? Answer against me, and I will repay you.”
They said to Samuel, “You have not wronged us or tyrannized us or crushed us, and you have taken nothing from anyone’s hand.”
Samuel said to the people, “The Lord is witness among you, and His anointed is witness today, on this day, that you have found nothing in my hand.” They said, “Witness.”

rationale: Sirach recalls Samuel speaking from the earth after death to announce the king's end. The narrative identifies the figure rising from the earth as Samuel and records his warning that Saul and his sons would fall and Israel's camp would be handed to its enemies.
source_text: Even after he fell asleep, he prophesied and showed the king his end. He raised his voice from the earth in prophecy to wipe out the people’s lawlessness.

target_units.text: The king said to her, “Do not fear. Tell me whom you have seen.” She said to him, “I have seen gods coming up from the earth.”

He said to her, “What did you perceive?” She said to him, “A man standing upright is coming up from the earth, wrapped in a double cloak.” Saul knew that this was Samuel, and he bent with his face to the ground and bowed to him.

Samuel said, “Why have you troubled me, that I should come up?” Saul said, “I am greatly afflicted. The foreigners are fighting against me, and God has departed from me and no longer listens to me, either through the prophets or by dreams. Now I have called you to make known to me what I should do.”
Samuel said, “Why do you inquire of me, when the Lord has departed from you and has come to be with your neighbour?
The Lord has done to you as He spoke by my hand. The Lord will tear your kingdom from your hand and give it to your neighbour David.
Because you did not listen to the Lord’s voice and did not carry out His furious anger against Amalek, the Lord has done this thing to you this day.
The Lord will hand Israel with you into the foreigners’ hands. Tomorrow you and your sons with you will fall. The Lord will give Israel’s camp into the foreigners’ hands.”

rationale: Sirach compares David's selection from Israel with fat set apart from a peace offering. Leviticus directs the removal of specified fat from the sacrifice of deliverance and its offering on the altar, supplying the sacrificial action used in the comparison.
source_text: As fat is set apart from a peace offering, so David was set apart from the sons of Israel.

target_units.text: And from the sacrifice of deliverance they shall bring an offering unto the Lord: the fat which covers the belly, and all the fat upon the belly,
and the two kidneys, and the fat upon them which is by the thighs, and the lobe upon the liver, which he shall remove with the kidneys.
And the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall offer them up upon the altar, upon the whole burnt offerings, upon the wood upon the fire upon the altar: an offering, a sweet savour unto the Lord.

rationale: Sirach describes David as set apart from Israel. The anointing narrative distinguishes David from Jesse's other sons: the Lord has not chosen those presented earlier, but expressly directs Samuel to anoint David.
source_text: As fat is set apart from a peace offering, so David was set apart from the sons of Israel.

target_units.text: Jesse made his seven sons pass before Samuel. Samuel said, “The Lord has not chosen among these.”

Samuel said to Jesse, “Are these all the boys?” He said, “There is still the youngest; he is tending the flock.” Samuel said to Jesse, “Send and fetch him, for we will certainly not recline until he comes.”
He sent and brought him. He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes, and good to look upon before the Lord. The Lord said to Samuel, “Rise and anoint David, for this one is good.”
Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him among his brothers. The Lord’s Spirit leaped upon David from that day onward. Samuel rose and went to Armathaim.

rationale: Sirach's image of David handling lions and bears recalls his account of protecting his father's flock. David tells Saul that he struck both lion and bear and rescued a sheep, crediting the Lord with his deliverance.
source_text: He played with lions as with young goats, and with bears as with lambs of the flock.

target_units.text: David said to Saul, “Your servant tended his father’s flock. Whenever a lion or a bear came and took a sheep from the herd,
I went after it, struck it, and pulled the sheep from its mouth. If it rose against me, I seized its throat, struck it, and killed it.

Your servant struck both bear and lion. The uncircumcised foreigner will be like one of them. Shall I not go and strike him and remove disgrace from Israel today? For who is this uncircumcised man who has defied the battle line of the living God?
The Lord, who rescued me from the lion’s paw and the bear’s paw, will rescue me from this uncircumcised foreigner’s hand.” Saul said to David, “Go, and the Lord will be with you.”

rationale: Sirach names the youthful David, his sling stone, and Goliath's defeat. The narrative describes David choosing stones, Goliath despising him as a boy, and David slinging a stone into the warrior's forehead.
source_text: In his youth did he not kill a giant and remove reproach from the people, when he raised his hand with a sling stone and brought down Goliath’s pride?

target_units.text: He took his staff in his hand, chose five smooth stones from the wadi, and put them in the shepherd’s little vessel he had for collecting. His sling was in his hand, and he approached the foreign man.
Goliath saw David and dishonoured him, for he was a boy, ruddy, with beautiful eyes.
The foreigner said to David, “Am I like a dog, that you come against me with a staff and stones?” David said, “No, you are worse than a dog.” The foreigner cursed David by his gods.
The foreigner said to David, “Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of heaven and the animals of the land.”
David said to the foreigner, “You come to me with sword, spear, and shield. I come to you in the name of the Lord Sabaoth, God of Israel’s battle line, which you have defied today.

This day the Lord will shut you into my hand. I will kill you and remove your head from you. This day I will give your limbs and the limbs of the foreigners’ camp to the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth, and all the earth will know that there is a God in Israel.
All this assembly will know that the Lord does not save by sword and spear. The battle belongs to the Lord, and the Lord will hand you all into our hands.”
The foreigner rose and went to meet David.

David reached his hand into the little vessel, took one stone from it, slung it, and struck the foreigner on his forehead. The stone passed through the helmet into his forehead, and he fell face down to the ground.

rationale: Sirach credits the Lord with David's victory over the mighty warrior. David's speech to Goliath expressly invokes the Lord's name and says the Lord will deliver the enemy into his hand because the battle belongs to the Lord.
source_text: For he called upon the Lord Most High, and He put strength in his right hand to remove a mighty warrior and raise the horn of His people.

rationale: Sirach recalls David being glorified with tens of thousands. The women's victory song assigns Saul thousands and David tens of thousands, and Saul's reaction confirms that this was praise of David's achievement.
source_text: Thus they glorified him with tens of thousands and praised him with blessings of the Lord when a crown of glory was brought to him.

target_units.text: The dancing women came out from all Israel’s cities to meet David, with tambourines, joy, and cymbals.
The women led the song and said, “Saul has struck his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.”
The saying appeared evil in Saul’s eyes concerning this matter, and he said, “They have given David the tens of thousands, but to me they have given the thousands.”
Saul kept looking askance at David from that day onward.

rationale: Sirach summarizes David's victories over his Philistine adversaries. The narrative describes two enemy advances after his anointing, his inquiries to the Lord, and the resulting defeats; this edition calls the opponents foreigners.
source_text: For he destroyed enemies all around and reduced his Philistine adversaries to nothing; he shattered their horn to this day.

target_units.text: The foreigners heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, and all the foreigners went up to seek David. David heard and went down to the stronghold.
The foreigners arrived and gathered in the Valley of the Titans.

David inquired through the Lord, saying, “Shall I go up against the foreigners? Wilt Thou deliver them into my hands?” The Lord said to David, “Go up, for I will certainly deliver the foreigners into your hands.”

David came from the Upper Breaches and struck the foreigners there. David said, “The Lord has broken through my enemies, the foreigners, before me as waters break through.” Therefore that place was named Upper Breaches.
They abandoned their gods there, and David and the men with him took them.
The foreigners came up again and gathered in the Valley of the Titans.
David inquired through the Lord, and the Lord said, “Do not go up to meet them. Turn away from them, and you will come upon them near the place of weeping.
When you hear the sound of the closing together of the grove of weeping, then go down against them, for then the Lord will go out before you to strike in the battle with the foreigners.”
David did as the Lord commanded him and struck the foreigners from Gibeon as far as the land of Gezer.

rationale: Sirach's summary of David reducing his adversaries recalls the compact narrative statement that David struck and routed the foreigners and took territory from their hand.
source_text: For he destroyed enemies all around and reduced his Philistine adversaries to nothing; he shattered their horn to this day.

target_units.text: After this, David struck the foreigners and routed them. David took the separated territory from the foreigners’ hand.

rationale: Sirach praises David's love for his Maker and songs of thanksgiving. The psalm's heading identifies David's song after deliverance from his enemies, and its opening expresses love for the Lord and praise of Him as helper and salvation.
source_text: In every deed he gave thanks to the Holy Most High with a word of glory. With his whole heart he sang hymns and loved the One who made him.

target_units.text: For the end. Of the Lord’s servant David, who spoke the words of this song to the Lord on the day the Lord rescued him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.
And he said: I will love Thee, Lord, my strength.
The Lord is my firm foundation, my refuge, and my rescuer; my God is my helper, and I will hope in Him; my protector, the horn of my salvation, my supporter.
Praising, I will call upon the Lord, and I will be saved from my enemies.

rationale: Sirach describes David giving thanks and glory to the Most High. Chronicles records David publicly blessing the Lord, acknowledging His power and glory, and explicitly giving thanks and praise to His glorious name.
source_text: In every deed he gave thanks to the Holy Most High with a word of glory. With his whole heart he sang hymns and loved the One who made him.

target_units.text: King David blessed the Lord before the assembly, saying, “Blessed art Thou, O Lord, the God of Israel, our Father, from everlasting to everlasting.
Thine, O Lord, are greatness, power, glory, victory, and strength; for Thou rulest all things in heaven and upon earth. Before Thee every king and nation is shaken.
From Thee come wealth and glory. Thou governest all, O Lord, Ruler of every rule. In Thy hand are strength and dominion; and it is in Thy hand, O Almighty, to make all things great and strong.
Now, O Lord, we give thanks unto Thee, and praise the name of Thy glory.

rationale: Sirach credits David with stationing psalm singers. Chronicles records his appointment of Levites to give thanks and praise with instruments, then names David's first appointment of praise through Asaph and his brethren.
source_text: He stationed psalm singers before the altar, to sweeten the melodies with their sound.

target_units.text: He appointed some Levites to minister before the ark of the Lord’s covenant, to sound out, give thanks, and praise the Lord, Israel’s God:
Asaph the leader, Zacharias second to him, Jiiel, Semiramoth, Jiiel, Mattathias, Eliab, Banaias, Abdedom, and Jiiel, with instruments, harps, and lyres; Asaph sounded the cymbals.
Banaias and Oziel the priests sounded trumpets continually before the ark of God’s covenant.
On that day David first appointed praise of the Lord through Asaph and his brethren:

rationale: Sirach places singers before the altar to sweeten the melodies. Chronicles' account of David's arrangements associates the priests and continual altar offerings with named singers, cymbals, trumpets, and instruments for God's songs.
source_text: He stationed psalm singers before the altar, to sweeten the melodies with their sound.

target_units.text: They left Sadok the priest and his brother priests before the Lord’s tent at Bama in Gabaon,

to present whole burnt offerings to the Lord continually on the altar of whole burnt offerings, morning and evening, according to everything written in the Lord’s law, all He commanded Israel’s sons through Moses, God’s attendant;
With him were Aiman, Idithon, and the remaining men chosen by name, to praise the Lord, for His mercy endures for ever.
With them were trumpets and cymbals for sounding out, and instruments for God’s songs; Idithon’s sons were at the gate.

rationale: Sirach joins David's ordering of festivals with praise resounding from early morning. The Levitical duties in Chronicles explicitly include morning and evening praise and the offerings for sabbaths, new moons, and feasts.
source_text: He gave festivals splendor and adorned the appointed seasons to their completion, while they praised His holy name and made the sanctuary resound from early morning.

target_units.text: and to stand in the morning to praise and give thanks unto the Lord, and likewise in the evening;
and over all the whole burnt offerings offered to the Lord on sabbaths, new moons, and feasts, by number according to the ordinance concerning them, continually for the Lord.

rationale: Sirach says the Lord removed David's sins. After David confesses to Nathan, the prophet expressly tells him that the Lord has put away his sin.
source_text: The Lord took away his sins, raised his horn for ever, and gave him a covenant of kings and a throne of glory in Israel.

target_units.text: David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the Lord.” Nathan said to David, “The Lord also has put away your sin; you will certainly not die.

rationale: Sirach refers to a covenant of kings and a glorious throne given to David. Nathan's oracle promises David an established successor, enduring mercy, and a house, kingdom, and throne made sure for ever.
source_text: The Lord took away his sins, raised his horn for ever, and gave him a covenant of kings and a throne of glory in Israel.

target_units.text: When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, who will be from your own body, and prepare his kingdom.
He will build Me a house for My name, and I will set his throne upright for ever.
I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to Me. If his wrongdoing comes, I will correct him with the rod of men and the afflictions of human beings.
But I will not withdraw My mercy from him as I withdrew it from those whom I removed from before Me.
His house and his kingdom will be made sure for ever before Me, and his throne will be set upright for ever.’”

rationale: Sirach describes the Lord raising David's horn for ever. The psalm uses the same royal image when the Lord promises to make a horn spring up for David, with a lamp for His anointed and shame for his enemies.
source_text: The Lord took away his sins, raised his horn for ever, and gave him a covenant of kings and a throne of glory in Israel.

target_units.text: There I will make a horn spring up for David; I have prepared a lamp for My anointed.
I will clothe his enemies with shame, but upon him My holy sign will blossom.”

rationale: Sirach introduces the son who arose after David. Kings narrates David's death and Solomon's accession to his father's throne, adding that Solomon's kingdom was firmly prepared.
source_text: After him arose a knowledgeable son, who because of him rested in spacious prosperity.

target_units.text: David lay down with his fathers and was buried in the City of David.
David’s reign over Israel lasted forty years. He reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
Solomon sat on the throne of his father David when he was twelve years old, and his kingdom was firmly prepared.

rationale: Sirach connects Solomon's peace and rest on every side with building a house for God's name. Solomon's message to Hiram makes precisely that connection: David's wars prevented the work, but the Lord has now given rest and Solomon intends to build.
source_text: Solomon reigned in days of peace; God gave him rest all around, so that he might establish a house for His name and prepare a sanctuary for ever.

target_units.text: “You know that my father David could not build a house for the name of the Lord my God because of the wars that surrounded him, until the Lord put them beneath the footsteps of his feet.
But now the Lord my God has given me rest on every side; there is no plotter and no evil encounter.

Behold, I intend to build a house for the name of the Lord my God, as the Lord God told my father David: ‘Your son, whom I shall place on your throne in your place, shall build the house for My name.’

rationale: Sirach's peaceful reign and sanctuary building correspond to the promise David recounts for Solomon. The promised son is a man of rest, Israel receives peace in his days, and he is to build a house for the Lord's name.
source_text: Solomon reigned in days of peace; God gave him rest all around, so that he might establish a house for His name and prepare a sanctuary for ever.

target_units.text: Behold, a son is born unto you; he shall be a man of rest. I will give him rest from all the enemies round about him, for Solomon is his name; and I will give peace and quietness unto Israel in his days.
He will build a house for My name. He will be a son to Me, and I will be a Father to him. I will set upright the throne of his kingdom in Israel for ever.’

rationale: Sirach praises Solomon's wisdom in youth. Solomon calls himself a little child and asks for understanding to judge; the Lord answers by giving him a discerning and wise heart.
source_text: How wise you became in your youth! You were filled with understanding like a river.

target_units.text: Now, Lord my God, Thou hast placed Thy servant in place of my father David. I am a little child and do not know my going out or my coming in.
Thy servant is among Thy people whom Thou didst choose, a numerous people who cannot be numbered.
Give Thy servant a heart to hear and to judge Thy people in righteousness, discerning between good and evil; for who can judge this weighty people of Thine?”
It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this.
The Lord said to him, “Because you have asked this of Me and have not asked for many days for yourself, or wealth, or the lives of your enemies, but have asked for understanding to hear judgment,
behold, I have done according to your word. Behold, I have given you a discerning and wise heart, so that no one like you has been before you, and no one like you shall arise after you.

rationale: Sirach describes Solomon as filled with understanding. Chronicles records his request for wisdom and understanding and God's explicit grant of both, supplying the parallel account of that gift.
source_text: How wise you became in your youth! You were filled with understanding like a river.

target_units.text: Now give me wisdom and understanding, and I shall go out before this people and come in; for who can judge this great people of Thine?”

God said to Solomon, “Because this came into your heart, and you did not ask for wealth of possessions, glory, or the life of opponents, and did not ask for many days, but did ask for wisdom and understanding to judge My people over whom I made you king,
I give you wisdom and understanding. I will also give you wealth, possessions, and glory, so that none like you has existed among the kings before you, nor will it be so after you.”

rationale: Sirach links Solomon's wide influence with comparisons and riddles. Kings enumerates his parables and songs, describes his discourse about living things, and says peoples came to hear his wisdom.
source_text: Your soul covered the earth, and you filled it with comparisons containing riddles.

target_units.text: Solomon spoke three thousand parables, and his songs numbered five thousand.
He spoke about trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop growing through the wall. He spoke about livestock, birds, creeping things, and fish.
All the peoples came to hear Solomon’s wisdom, and he received gifts from all the kings of the earth who had heard of his wisdom.

rationale: Sirach celebrates Solomon's name reaching distant places. The queen of Sheba hears of his name in her own land, travels to question him, and declares that his discernment surpasses the report she had heard; this is a particular example of his foreign renown.
source_text: Your name reached distant islands, and you were loved for your peace.

target_units.text: The queen of Sheba heard Solomon’s name and the Lord’s name, and came to test him with riddles.
She came to Jerusalem with a very great retinue, with camels carrying spices, very much gold, and precious stones. She came in to Solomon and spoke to him about everything in her heart.
Solomon explained all her matters to her. No matter was overlooked by the king that he did not explain to her.
When the queen of Sheba saw all Solomon’s discernment and the house he had built,
Solomon’s food, the seating of his attendants, the station of his ministers, his clothing, his wine-pourers, and his whole burnt offering which he offered in the Lord’s house, she was beside herself.
She said to King Solomon, “The report I heard in my land about your word and your discernment is true.
I did not believe those speaking to me until I arrived and my eyes saw. Behold, it is not half as they reported to me! You have added good things beyond them, beyond every report I heard in my land.

rationale: Sirach associates the countries' admiration with Solomon's songs and wise sayings. Kings enumerates his songs and parables, says that peoples came to hear his wisdom, and adds that he received gifts from kings who had heard of it.
source_text: Countries marveled at you for songs, proverbs, comparisons, and interpretations.

rationale: Sirach says countries marveled at Solomon's interpretations. Chronicles describes the queen of Saba testing him with riddles, receiving explanations of every question, and declaring that the abundance of his wisdom exceeded its reputation.
source_text: Countries marveled at you for songs, proverbs, comparisons, and interpretations.

target_units.text: The queen of Saba heard Solomon’s name and came to Jerusalem to test Solomon with riddles, with a very great force and camels carrying spices, plentiful gold, and precious stones. She came to Solomon and spoke to him about everything in her soul.
Solomon explained all her questions to her. No matter escaped Solomon that he did not explain to her.
When the queen of Saba saw Solomon’s wisdom and the house he had built,

the food of the tables, the seating of his servants, the station of his ministers and their clothing, his wine-pourers and their attire, and the whole burnt offerings he offered in the Lord’s house, she was beside herself.
She said to the king, “The report I heard in my land about your words and wisdom was true.
I did not believe the words until I came and my eyes saw. Behold, not half the abundance of your wisdom was reported to me! You surpass the report I heard.

rationale: Sirach portrays gold and silver as extraordinarily plentiful under Solomon. Kings describes golden vessels, silver having no value in his days, and ships bringing gold and silver, illustrating the abundance behind Sirach's metal comparisons.
source_text: In the name of the Lord God, who is called the God of Israel, you gathered gold like tin and multiplied silver like lead.

target_units.text: All Solomon’s drinking vessels were gold, and the basins were gold. All the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were encased in gold. None were silver, because silver was not valued in Solomon’s days.
For the king had a Tarshish ship at sea with Hiram’s ships. Once every three years a ship came to the king from Tarshish with gold, silver, and engraved and hewn stones.

rationale: Sirach compares Solomon's plentiful gold and silver with tin and lead. Chronicles similarly describes those precious metals becoming as common as stones in Jerusalem; the comparison changes, but the asserted abundance is the same.
source_text: In the name of the Lord God, who is called the God of Israel, you gathered gold like tin and multiplied silver like lead.

target_units.text: The king made gold and silver in Jerusalem like stones, and cedars as plentiful as sycamores in the plain.

rationale: Sirach addresses Solomon's submission to women. Kings names his many wives and concubines and says that his foreign wives turned his heart after their gods, explaining the compromise recalled by Sirach.
source_text: You bent your loins toward women and were brought under power in your body.

target_units.text: King Solomon was a lover of women. He had seven hundred princesses and three hundred concubines. He took foreign wives, as well as Pharaoh’s daughter: Moabite, Ammonite, Syrian, Edomite, Hittite, and Amorite women,

from the nations about which the Lord had forbidden the sons of Israel, “You shall not go in among them, and they shall not come in among you, lest they turn your hearts after their idols.” Solomon clung to these in love.
When Solomon was old, his heart was not whole with the Lord his God, as was the heart of David his father; the foreign wives turned his heart after their gods.

rationale: Sirach recalls Solomon being brought under women's power. Nehemiah likewise appeals to Solomon's example, saying that despite his greatness and God's love for him, foreign women turned him aside.
source_text: You bent your loins toward women and were brought under power in your body.

target_units.text: “Did not Salomon king of Israel sin in this way? Among many nations there was no king like him, and he was loved by God, and God made him king over all Israel. Yet foreign women turned even him aside.

rationale: Sirach connects Solomon's failure with wrath falling on his children. Kings records the Lord's anger and the announcement that the kingdom would be torn away from Solomon's son's hand, with an exception made for David's sake.
source_text: You put a blemish upon your glory and profaned your offspring, bringing wrath upon your children and anguish because of your folly,

target_units.text: The Lord became angry with Solomon because he had turned his heart away from the Lord, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice
and had commanded him about this matter, absolutely not to follow other gods, and to take care to do what the Lord God had commanded him.

The Lord said to Solomon, “Because these things have been your conduct, and you have not kept My commandments and My ordinances which I commanded you, I will surely tear your kingdom from your hand and give it to your servant.
Yet I will not do these things in your days, because of David your father. I will take it from your son’s hand.
But I will certainly not take the whole kingdom. I will give your son one scepter, because of David My servant and because of Jerusalem, the city I have chosen.”

rationale: Sirach recalls the divided dominion and a separate disobedient kingdom. Kings narrates Israel's rejection of David's house and its installation of Jeroboam as king, while Judah and Benjamin remain with David's house.
source_text: so that the dominion became divided and a disobedient kingdom began from Ephraim.

target_units.text: All Israel saw that the king had not listened to them. The people answered the king, “What share have we in David? We have no inheritance in Jesse’s son. Run away to your tents, Israel! Now shepherd your own house, David!” Israel went to their tents.
The king sent Adoniram, who supervised the tribute. All Israel stoned him with stones, and he died. King Rehoboam managed to go up and flee to Jerusalem.
Israel rejected David’s house, as it remains to this day.

When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned from Egypt, they sent and called him to the assembly and made him king over Israel. None followed David’s house except Judah’s scepter and Benjamin alone.

rationale: Sirach insists that the Lord's mercy and word will not fail and that David's descendants will not be wiped out. The psalm promises enduring mercy, a faithful covenant, and David's seed and throne continuing despite correction of his sons' sins.
source_text: But the Lord will never abandon His mercy or let any of His words fail. He will never wipe out His chosen one’s descendants or remove the offspring of the one who loved Him. He gave Jacob a remnant, and David a root from him.

target_units.text: For ever I will keep My mercy for him, and My covenant is faithful to him.
I will establish his seed for an age of an age and his throne like the days of heaven.
If his sons abandon My law and do not walk in My judgments,
if they profane My ordinances and do not keep My commandments,
I will visit their lawless acts with a rod and their sins with scourges;
but I shall certainly not scatter My mercy away from him, nor act unjustly in My truth,
nor shall I profane My covenant, and what goes out through My lips I shall certainly not set aside.
Once I swore by My holiness: I will not lie to David.
His seed will remain for ever, and his throne will be like the sun before Me,
and like the moon, established for ever; and the witness in heaven is faithful.” Diapsalma.

rationale: Sirach says the Lord preserved descendants and a remnant despite royal failure. The judgment on Solomon expressly leaves his son a scepter for David's sake and for Jerusalem, illustrating preservation within the announced division.
source_text: But the Lord will never abandon His mercy or let any of His words fail. He will never wipe out His chosen one’s descendants or remove the offspring of the one who loved Him. He gave Jacob a remnant, and David a root from him.

rationale: Sirach attributes the revolt under Rehoboam to his deficient counsel. Kings shows him rejecting the elders' advice, following the young men's harsh counsel, and provoking Israel's declaration that it has no share in David's house.
source_text: Solomon rested with his fathers and left after him, from his offspring, the people’s foolishness: Rehoboam, deficient in understanding, who made the people revolt through his counsel.

target_units.text: The king instructed the elders who had stood before Solomon his father while he was still alive, saying, “How do you advise me, so that I may answer this people?”
They said to him, “If this day you become this people’s servant, serve them, and speak good words to them, they will be your servants always.”
He abandoned the elders’ counsel which they had given him and consulted the young men who had been brought up with him and stood before him.
He said to them, “What do you advise, and what shall I answer this people who said to me, ‘Lighten the collar your father placed on us’?”

The young men who had been brought up with him and stood before him said, “Thus speak to this people who told you, ‘Your father made our collar heavy; now lighten it for us.’ Thus speak to them: ‘My little part is thicker than my father’s loins.
Now my father burdened you with a heavy collar, but I will add to your collar. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.’”
All Israel came to King Rehoboam on the third day, as the king had told them, “Return to me on the third day.”
The king answered the people harshly, and Rehoboam abandoned the elders’ counsel which they had given him.

He spoke to them according to the young men’s counsel: “My father made your collar heavy, but I will add to your collar. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.”
The king did not listen to the people, for the turn of events came from the Lord, to establish His word which He had spoken through Ahijah the Shilonite concerning Jeroboam son of Nebat.

All Israel saw that the king had not listened to them. The people answered the king, “What share have we in David? We have no inheritance in Jesse’s son. Run away to your tents, Israel! Now shepherd your own house, David!” Israel went to their tents.

rationale: Sirach's charge against Rehoboam corresponds to Chronicles' account of the same consultation and revolt: the elders recommend kindness, he follows the younger men instead, answers harshly, and the people depart to their dwellings.
source_text: Solomon rested with his fathers and left after him, from his offspring, the people’s foolishness: Rehoboam, deficient in understanding, who made the people revolt through his counsel.

target_units.text: King Rehoboam gathered the elders who had stood before Solomon his father while he was alive: “How do you advise answering this people?”
They told him, “If today you are good to this people, show favor, and speak good words to them, they will be your servants all the days.”
He abandoned the elders’ counsel that they had given him and consulted the young men brought up with him who stood before him.
He said to them, “What do you advise, that I may answer this people who said to me, ‘Relax the yoke your father placed upon us’?”

The young men brought up with him told him, “Speak this way to the people who said to you, ‘Your father made our yoke heavy; you release us from it.’ Say this: ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s loins.
My father disciplined you with a heavy yoke; I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips; I will discipline you with scorpions.’”
Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam on the third day, as the king had said, “Return to me on the third day.”
The king answered harshly. King Rehoboam abandoned the elders’ counsel,
and spoke to them according to the younger men’s counsel: “My father made your yoke heavy, and I will add to it. My father disciplined you with whips; I will discipline you with scorpions.”
The king did not listen to the people, for there was a reversal from God, saying, “The Lord established His word that He spoke through Achia the Selonite concerning Jeroboam son of Nabat

and all Israel,” because the king did not listen to them. The people answered the king: “What share have we in David, and what inheritance in Jesse’s son? To your dwellings, Israel! Now see to your house, David!” All Israel went to their dwellings.

rationale: Sirach says Jeroboam made Israel sin and provided a path of sin. Kings describes his golden heifers, shrines, unauthorized priestly appointments, and invented feast, explicitly calling the matter a sin.
source_text: There was also Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin and gave Ephraim a path of sin. Their sins multiplied exceedingly, so that they were removed from their land.

target_units.text: The king took counsel, went, and made two golden heifers. He said to the people, “Let your going up to Jerusalem be enough. Behold, your gods, Israel, who brought you up from Egypt!”
He placed one in Bethel and put the other in Dan.
This matter became a sin. The people went before the one as far as Dan.
He made houses on high places and appointed some of the people as priests who were not from the sons of Levi.

Jeroboam held a feast in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, like the feast in the land of Judah, and went up onto the altar he had made in Bethel to sacrifice to the heifers he had made. He stationed in Bethel the priests of the high places he had made.

He went up onto the altar he had made, on the fifteenth day in the eighth month, at the feast he had fashioned from his heart. He held a feast for the sons of Israel and went up onto the altar to offer sacrifice.

rationale: Sirach connects Jeroboam's influence with Israel's eventual removal from its land. Kings explicitly says that Jeroboam thrust Israel away from the Lord, that Israel persisted in his sins, and that the nation was deported to Assyria.
source_text: There was also Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin and gave Ephraim a path of sin. Their sins multiplied exceedingly, so that they were removed from their land.

target_units.text: For Israel was apart from David’s house, and they made Jeroboam son of Nebat king. Jeroboam thrust Israel away from following the Lord and caused them to commit a great sin.
The Israelites walked in every sin Jeroboam committed; they did not turn away from it,
until the Lord removed Israel from His presence, as the Lord had spoken through all His servants the prophets. Israel was deported from its land to the Assyrians, to this day.

rationale: Sirach describes accumulating wickedness until vengeance came. Kings recounts the rejected prophetic warnings, the abandonment of the commandments and idolatrous practices, and the Lord's anger and removal of Israel.
source_text: They sought out every kind of wickedness, until vengeance came upon them.

target_units.text: The Lord warned Israel and Judah through all His prophets, every seer: ‘Turn from your evil ways and keep My commandments, My ordinances, and all the law I commanded your fathers, all that I sent to them through My servants the prophets.’
But they did not listen. They hardened their back more than the back of their fathers.

They did not keep His testimonies by which He warned them. They followed vain things and became vain, and followed the nations around them, concerning whom He had commanded them not to do such things.
They abandoned the commandments of the Lord their God. They made a casting for themselves, two heifers, made groves, bowed down to all heaven’s host, and served Baal.
They led their sons and daughters through fire, practiced divinations, read omens, and were sold to do evil in the Lord’s eyes, provoking Him.
The Lord was very angry with Israel and removed them from His presence. None remained except the tribe of Judah alone.

rationale: Sirach compares Elijah's prophetic word to a burning torch. Jeremiah contrasts dreams with the Lord's true word and compares that word to blazing fire; the parallel concerns the force of prophetic speech, while the prophets are different.
source_text: Then Elijah arose, a prophet like fire, and his word burned like a torch.

target_units.text: Let the prophet in whom there is a dream tell his dream, and the one to whom My word comes tell My word in truth. What has chaff to do with wheat? So are My words, says the Lord.
Are not My words like blazing fire, says the Lord, and like an axe cutting rock?

rationale: Sirach recalls Elijah bringing famine upon the people. Kings places a severe famine in Samaria within Elijah's ministry and records the Lord's instruction that Elijah appear before Ahab as rain is promised.
source_text: He brought famine upon them and made them few through his zeal.

target_units.text: After many days, the Lord’s word came to Elijah in the third year, saying, “Go and show yourself to Ahab, and I will give rain on the face of the land.”
Elijah went to show himself to Ahab. The famine was severe in Samaria.

rationale: Sirach remembers the famine in Elijah's days. Jesus likewise recalls heaven being shut and a great famine during Elijah's ministry, adding the particular episode of his being sent to the widow in Sidon's territory.
source_text: He brought famine upon them and made them few through his zeal.

target_units.text: But in truth I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in Elijah’s days, when heaven was shut for three years and six months and a great famine came over the whole land.
Yet Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow at Zarephath in Sidon’s territory.

rationale: Sirach says Elijah shut heaven by the Lord's word. Elijah's declaration to Ahab in Kings explicitly withholds dew and rain except through the utterance of his word, under oath by the living God of Israel.
source_text: By the Lord’s word he held back heaven; in the same way he brought down fire three times.

target_units.text: Elijah the prophet, the Tishbite from Thesbon in Gilead, said to Ahab, “As the Lord, the God of hosts, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there will be neither dew nor rain these years except through the utterance of my word.”

rationale: Sirach recalls Elijah bringing down fire from heaven. Kings narrates one such occasion: Elijah appeals to the Lord with fire, fire consumes the offering and its surroundings, and the people confess the Lord as God.
source_text: By the Lord’s word he held back heaven; in the same way he brought down fire three times.

target_units.text: Elijah cried out to heaven and said, “Lord, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, hear me, Lord! Hear me this day with fire, and let all this people know that Thou art the Lord, the God of Israel, and I am Thy servant, and that I have done these works because of Thee.
Hear me, Lord! Hear me with fire, and let this people know that Thou art the Lord God, and that Thou hast turned this people’s heart backward.”
Fire from the Lord fell from heaven and consumed the burnt offering, the split wood, and the water in the trench; the fire licked up the stones and the dust.
All the people fell on their faces and said, “Truly the Lord is God! He is God!”

rationale: Sirach's account of fire descending through Elijah is supported by Kings' two successive episodes in which fire consumes a captain and his fifty men.
source_text: By the Lord’s word he held back heaven; in the same way he brought down fire three times.

target_units.text: He sent to him a commander, a captain of fifty, with his fifty men. He went up and came to him, and there Elijah was, sitting on the top of the mountain. The captain of fifty spoke to him and said, ‘Man of God, the king has summoned you. Come down!’

Elijah answered and said to the captain of fifty, ‘If I am a man of God, fire will come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men.’ Fire came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty men.
The king again sent to him another captain of fifty with his fifty men. The captain went up and spoke to him, saying, ‘Man of God, thus says the king: Come down quickly!’
Elijah answered and spoke to him, saying, ‘If I am a man of God, fire will come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men.’ Fire came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty men.

rationale: Sirach associates Elijah with heaven being shut. James expressly names Elijah, describes his earnest prayer that rain cease, and contrasts the ensuing drought with the rain and fruitfulness following his later prayer.
source_text: By the Lord’s word he held back heaven; in the same way he brought down fire three times.

target_units.text: Elijah was a human being with experiences like ours, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain; and it did not rain upon the earth for three years and six months.
And he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth brought forth its fruit.

rationale: Sirach praises Elijah's remarkable wonders. The fire answering his appeal in Kings provides a concrete example of those wonders, with the people falling before God after the offering, water, stones, and dust are consumed.
source_text: How glorious you became, Elijah, through your wonders! Who can boast of being like you?

target_units.text: Elijah cried out to heaven and said, “Lord, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, hear me, Lord! Hear me this day with fire, and let all this people know that Thou art the Lord, the God of Israel, and I am Thy servant, and that I have done these works because of Thee.
Hear me, Lord! Hear me with fire, and let this people know that Thou art the Lord God, and that Thou hast turned this people’s heart backward.”
Fire from the Lord fell from heaven and consumed the burnt offering, the split wood, and the water in the trench; the fire licked up the stones and the dust.
All the people fell on their faces and said, “Truly the Lord is God! He is God!”

rationale: Sirach credits Elijah with raising a dead person. Kings recounts the widow's breathless son, Elijah's prayer that the child's soul return, and his presentation of the living child to his mother.
source_text: You raised a dead man from death and from Hades by the word of the Most High.

target_units.text: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, became ill. His illness was very severe, until no breath remained in him.
She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, man of God? You have come to me to bring my wrongdoings to remembrance and to put my son to death!”
Elijah said to the woman, “Give me your son.” He took him from her bosom, carried him up to the upper room where he was staying, and laid him on his bed.
Elijah cried out and said, “Alas, Lord, Witness of the widow with whom I am staying—Thou hast brought harm by putting her son to death!”
He breathed into the child three times, called upon the Lord, and said, “Lord my God, I pray Thee, let this child’s soul return into him!”
It happened so, and the child cried out.
He brought him down from the upper room into the house and gave him to his mother. Elijah said, “Behold, your son lives!”
The woman said to Elijah, “Behold, I know that you are a man of God, and the Lord’s word in your mouth is true.”

rationale: Sirach speaks of Elijah bringing down rulers from their beds. Kings records his message that the king will not leave the bed of illness but will die, followed by the king's death according to that word.
source_text: You brought kings down to destruction and glorious men from their bed.

target_units.text: An angel of the Lord spoke to Elijah and said, ‘Go down with him; do not be afraid of them.’ Elijah rose and went down with him to the king.

Elijah spoke to him and said, ‘Thus says the Lord: Why did you send messengers to inquire of Baal Fly, the god of Ekron? It shall not be so! The bed onto which you have gone up—you will not come down from it, for you will surely die.’
He died according to the word of the Lord that Elijah had spoken.

rationale: Sirach recalls Elijah's judgments against kings. In this edition's chapter 20, Elijah confronts Ahab over Naboth's vineyard and announces calamity and the destruction of his house; the passage records the judgment announced, rather than its later execution.
source_text: You brought kings down to destruction and glorious men from their bed.

target_units.text: The Lord spoke to Elijah the Tishbite, saying,
“Rise and go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who is in Samaria. Behold, he is in Naboth’s vineyard, because he has gone down there to take possession of it.

Say to him, ‘Thus says the Lord: Because you did murder and did take possession, therefore thus says the Lord: In every place where swine and dogs licked Naboth’s blood, dogs will lick your blood there, and prostitutes will bathe in your blood.’”
Ahab said to Elijah, “Have you found me, my enemy?” He said, “I have found you, because you have been sold in vain to do evil before the Lord, provoking Him.

Thus says the Lord: ‘Behold, I am bringing calamities upon you. I will burn out what remains after you and destroy from Ahab every male who urinates against a wall, both confined and abandoned in Israel.
I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like the house of Baasha son of Ahijah, because of the provocations you have provoked and because you did cause Israel to sin.’”

rationale: Sirach recalls Elijah hearing rebuke and judgment at Horeb. Kings places Elijah at Mount Horeb, records the divine question about his presence there, and gives the ensuing commands concerning Hazael, Jehu, Elisha, and the ensuing judgments.
source_text: You heard rebuke at Sinai and judgments of vengeance at Horeb.

target_units.text: He rose, ate, and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Mount Horeb.
He entered the cave there and lodged there. Behold, the Lord’s word came to him, and He said, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

Elijah said, “I have been most zealous for the Lord Almighty, because the children of Israel have abandoned Thee. They have demolished Thine altars and killed Thy prophets with the sword. I remain utterly alone, and they seek my life to take it.”

He said, “You shall go out tomorrow and stand before the Lord on the mountain. Behold, the Lord will pass by.” A great, strong wind was breaking mountains apart and crushing rocks before the Lord, but the Lord was not in the wind. After the wind came an earthquake, but the Lord was not in the earthquake.
After the earthquake came a fire, but the Lord was not in the fire. After the fire came the sound of a gentle breeze, and there was the Lord.
When Elijah heard, he covered his face with his sheepskin cloak, went out, and stood beneath the cave. Behold, a voice came to him and said, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

Elijah said, “I have been most zealous for the Lord Almighty, because the children of Israel have forsaken Thy covenant. They have pulled down Thine altars and killed Thy prophets with the sword. I remain utterly alone, and they seek my life to take it.”
The Lord said to him, “Go, return on your way, and you will come to the wilderness road of Damascus. Anoint Hazael as king of Syria.
Anoint Jehu son of Nimshi as king over Israel, and anoint Elisha son of Shaphat, from Abel-meholah, as prophet in your place.
Whoever is spared from Hazael’s sword, Jehu will put to death; whoever is spared from Jehu’s sword, Elisha will put to death.

rationale: Sirach associates Elijah with kings appointed for retribution and a prophetic successor. Kings records the Lord commissioning the anointing of Hazael and Jehu, naming Elisha as prophet in Elijah's place, and describing the succeeding agents of judgment.
source_text: You anointed kings for retribution, and prophets as successors after him.

rationale: Sirach recalls Elijah's fiery departure. Kings describes the chariot and horses of fire separating Elijah and Elisha, Elijah's ascent in a tumult, and Elisha watching until he sees him no more.
source_text: You were taken up in a whirlwind of fire, in a chariot with fiery horses.

target_units.text: As they went, walking and speaking, behold—a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them, and Elijah was taken up in a tumult, as into heaven.
Elisha was watching and crying, ‘Father, father! Israel’s chariot and its horseman!’ He saw him no more. He seized his clothes and tore them into two pieces.

rationale: Sirach associates Elijah's appointed work with turning a father's heart toward a son before wrath. Malachi, at these native anchors, promises Elijah before the Lord's day and the restoration of a father's heart toward a son to avert the land's destruction.
source_text: You were recorded in rebukes for appointed times: to still anger before wrath, to turn a father’s heart toward a son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.

target_units.text: “And look, I am sending you Elijah the Tishbite before the coming of the Lord’s great and manifest day,
who will restore a father’s heart toward a son and a person’s heart toward his neighbor, lest I come and strike the land utterly.”

rationale: Sirach connects Elijah with restored hearts and Israel's restoration. Luke describes John's mission in Elijah's spirit and power as turning Israel to God and fathers' hearts toward children; this relates the missions without identifying John as the same person as Elijah.
source_text: You were recorded in rebukes for appointed times: to still anger before wrath, to turn a father’s heart toward a son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.

target_units.text: He will turn many of the sons of Israel to the Lord their God.

He himself will go before Him in Elijah’s spirit and power, to turn fathers’ hearts toward children and the disobedient to the understanding of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord a people made ready.”

rationale: Sirach recalls Elijah's appointed restorative task. Matthew records the expectation that Elijah restore all things and Jesus' interpretation concerning John the Baptist, preserving the Gospel's own distinction between the expectation and its interpretation.
source_text: You were recorded in rebukes for appointed times: to still anger before wrath, to turn a father’s heart toward a son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.

target_units.text: The disciples asked Him, “Why, then, do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”
He answered, “Elijah indeed comes and will restore all things.
But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they wished. In the same way the Son of Man is also to suffer at their hands.”
Then the disciples understood that He spoke to them about John the Baptist.

rationale: Sirach connects Elijah's departure with Elisha receiving his spirit. Kings narrates the departure, Elisha's subsequent division of the Jordan, and the prophetic community's declaration that Elijah's spirit has come to rest upon Elisha.
source_text: Elijah was covered by a whirlwind, and Elisha was filled with his spirit. In his days he was not shaken by a ruler, and no one overpowered him.

target_units.text: As they went, walking and speaking, behold—a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them, and Elijah was taken up in a tumult, as into heaven.
Elisha was watching and crying, ‘Father, father! Israel’s chariot and its horseman!’ He saw him no more. He seized his clothes and tore them into two pieces.
He picked up Elijah’s sheepskin, which had fallen upon Elisha, and Elisha returned and stood on the edge of the Jordan.

He took Elijah’s sheepskin, which had fallen upon him, and struck the water, but it did not separate. He said, ‘Where is the God of Elijah—Appho?’ He struck the waters, and they split to this side and that, and Elisha crossed over.
The sons of the prophets in Jericho saw him from opposite him and said, ‘The spirit of Elijah has come to rest upon Elisha.’ They came to meet him and bowed before him to the ground.

rationale: Sirach says Elisha was not shaken by a ruler. Kings supplies a particular example: Elisha confronts Israel's king, directs him to his father's prophets, and says he regards him only on account of Jehoshaphat.
source_text: Elijah was covered by a whirlwind, and Elisha was filled with his spirit. In his days he was not shaken by a ruler, and no one overpowered him.

target_units.text: Jehoshaphat said, ‘Is there no prophet of the Lord here, through whom we may inquire of the Lord?’ One of the attendants of the king of Israel answered, ‘Elisha son of Shaphat is here, who poured water on Elijah’s hands.’
Jehoshaphat said, ‘A word of the Lord is with him.’ The king of Israel, Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and the king of Edom went down to him.

Elisha said to the king of Israel, ‘What have I to do with you? Go to your father’s prophets.’ The king of Israel said to him, ‘No! For the Lord has called the three kings together to hand them over into the hands of Moab.’
Elisha said, ‘As the Lord of hosts lives, before whom I stand, if I were not showing regard for Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would neither look toward you nor see you.’

rationale: Sirach describes Elisha's body as prophetic even after death. Kings relates a dead man's revival upon touching Elisha's bones, providing the bodily wonder behind that description without reporting a spoken prophecy from the corpse.
source_text: No word surpassed him, and even in sleep his body prophesied.

target_units.text: Elisha died, and they buried him. Moab’s lightly equipped raiders came into the land when the year came round.
As they were burying the man, suddenly they saw the lightly equipped raider. They threw the man into Elisha’s grave. He went and touched Elisha’s bones, came to life, and stood on his feet.

rationale: Sirach praises Elisha's portents during life. Kings gives the concrete example of his prayer and actions over the Shunammite woman's dead child, who opens his eyes and is returned to his mother.
source_text: In his life he performed portents, and at his end his works were wondrous.

target_units.text: Elisha entered the house, and there was the child, dead, lying on his bed.
Elisha entered the house, shut the door behind the two of them, and prayed to the Lord.
He went up and lay upon the child, putting his mouth on his mouth, his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He bent over him, and the child’s flesh was warmed.
He returned and walked in the house this way and that. He went up and bent over the child as many as seven times, and the child opened his eyes.
Elisha called out to Gehazi and said, ‘Call this Shunammite woman.’ He called, and she came in to him. Elisha said, ‘Take your son.’
The woman came in, fell at his feet, and bowed to the ground. She took her son and went out.

rationale: Sirach distinguishes Elisha's wonders during life from those at his end. Kings' account of a man revived through contact with Elisha's bones supplies the posthumous counterpart to that contrast.
source_text: In his life he performed portents, and at his end his works were wondrous.

target_units.text: Elisha died, and they buried him. Moab’s lightly equipped raiders came into the land when the year came round.
