rationale: Sirach links refusal to repent with removal and scattering. Kings recounts Israel's refusal to heed prophetic warnings and its persistence in sins until the Lord removed Israel and it was deported to Assyria.
source_text: Through all these things the people did not repent or turn away from their sins, until they were plundered from their land and scattered throughout all the earth.

target_units.text: The Lord warned Israel and Judah through all His prophets, every seer: ‘Turn from your evil ways and keep My commandments, My ordinances, and all the law I commanded your fathers, all that I sent to them through My servants the prophets.’
But they did not listen. They hardened their back more than the back of their fathers.

They did not keep His testimonies by which He warned them. They followed vain things and became vain, and followed the nations around them, concerning whom He had commanded them not to do such things.
They abandoned the commandments of the Lord their God. They made a casting for themselves, two heifers, made groves, bowed down to all heaven’s host, and served Baal.
They led their sons and daughters through fire, practiced divinations, read omens, and were sold to do evil in the Lord’s eyes, provoking Him.
The Lord was very angry with Israel and removed them from His presence. None remained except the tribe of Judah alone.
Judah also did not keep the commandments of the Lord their God; they walked in the ordinances Israel had made.
They rejected the Lord throughout all Israel’s seed; He shook them and gave them into the hands of those plundering them, until He cast them from His presence.
For Israel was apart from David’s house, and they made Jeroboam son of Nebat king. Jeroboam thrust Israel away from following the Lord and caused them to commit a great sin.
The Israelites walked in every sin Jeroboam committed; they did not turn away from it,
until the Lord removed Israel from His presence, as the Lord had spoken through all His servants the prophets. Israel was deported from its land to the Assyrians, to this day.

rationale: Sirach recounts the unrepentant people's removal and scattering over the earth. Deuteronomy warns of removal from the inherited land and dispersion among nations from one end of the earth to the other, supplying the corresponding covenant consequence.
source_text: Through all these things the people did not repent or turn away from their sins, until they were plundered from their land and scattered throughout all the earth.

target_units.text: And it shall be, as the Lord rejoiced over you to do you good and to multiply you, so shall the Lord rejoice over you to destroy you; and you shall be removed from the land whither you go to inherit it.

And the Lord your God shall scatter you among all the nations, from one end of the earth unto the other; and there you shall serve other gods, wood and stone, which neither you nor your fathers have known.

rationale: Sirach describes a reduced remnant associated with David's ruling house and continuing disobedience. Kings says that only Judah remained after Israel's removal, then adds that Judah also failed to keep the Lord's commandments.
source_text: The people were left few in number, with a ruler in David’s house. Some of them did what was pleasing, but others multiplied sins.

rationale: Sirach remembers Hezekiah's works bringing water into the fortified city. Kings' concluding notice expressly records his fountain and aqueduct and the bringing of water into the city.
source_text: Hezekiah fortified his city and brought water into its midst. With iron he dug through a steep rock and built reservoirs for water.

target_units.text: The rest of Hezekiah’s deeds, all his might, and what he made—the fountain and aqueduct—and how he brought water into the city—are these not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?

rationale: Sirach combines Hezekiah's fortification and water works. Chronicles describes his response to the Assyrian threat through controlling nearby water, rebuilding the wall and towers, and adding an outer defensive wall.
source_text: Hezekiah fortified his city and brought water into its midst. With iron he dug through a steep rock and built reservoirs for water.

target_units.text: Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had arrived and that his face was set to wage war against Jerusalem.
He consulted with his elders and mighty men about blocking the waters of the springs outside the city, and they joined in strengthening him.
He gathered a great crowd and blocked the waters of the springs and the river that divided the city, saying, “Let the king of Assyria not come and find abundant water and gain strength.”
Hezekiah grew strong and built the entire demolished wall and towers, and outside another defensive wall. He strengthened the retaining work of the City of David and prepared many weapons.

rationale: Sirach names Sennacherib's invasion and his envoy Rabshakeh. Kings places Sennacherib's attack in Hezekiah's reign and sends the officer named Rhapsakes in this edition, with other officers and a large force, to Jerusalem.
source_text: In his days Sennacherib came up and sent Rabshakeh, and he departed. He raised his hand against Zion and boasted greatly in his arrogance.

target_units.text: In King Hezekiah’s fourteenth year, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians went up against Judah’s fortified cities and captured them.

Hezekiah king of Judah sent messengers to the king of the Assyrians at Lachish: ‘I have sinned. Withdraw from me; whatever you impose on me, I will bear.’ The king of the Assyrians imposed on Hezekiah king of Judah three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold.
Hezekiah gave all the silver found in the Lord’s house and in the treasuries of the king’s house.
At that time Hezekiah cut apart the doors of the Lord’s sanctuary and the fixed supports which Hezekiah king of Judah had gilded, and gave them to the king of the Assyrians.

The king of the Assyrians sent Tharthan, Raphis, and Rhapsakes from Lachish to King Hezekiah against Jerusalem with a great force. They went up, came to Jerusalem, and stood at the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road of the Fuller’s Field.

rationale: Sirach recalls the Assyrian king's envoy and his boastful challenge to Zion. Isaiah's parallel account names Sennacherib and the envoy Rapsakes, sends him to Jerusalem, and opens his challenge by invoking the authority of the great king.
source_text: In his days Sennacherib came up and sent Rabshakeh, and he departed. He raised his hand against Zion and boasted greatly in his arrogance.

target_units.text: In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah’s reign, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians came up against Judea’s fortified cities and took them.
The king of the Assyrians sent Rapsakes from Lachis to Jerusalem, to King Hezekiah, with a large force. He stood at the upper pool’s aqueduct, on the road of the fuller’s field.
Eliakim son of Chelkias, the steward, Somnas the scribe, and Joach son of Asaph, the record-keeper, went out to him.

rationale: Sirach compares the people's terror to birth pains. In the same Assyrian crisis, Hezekiah's messengers describe affliction through the image of children reaching birth when the mother has no strength to deliver.
source_text: Then their hearts and hands were shaken, and they suffered pangs like women giving birth.

target_units.text: When King Hezekiah heard, he tore his garments, put on sackcloth, and entered the Lord’s house.
He sent Eliakim the steward, Somnas the scribe, and the elders of the priests, clothed in sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet, son of Amos.
They said to him, ‘Thus says Hezekiah: This day is a day of affliction, rebuke, and provocation. Children have reached the birth pains, but the woman giving birth has no strength.

Perhaps the Lord your God will hear all Rhapsakes’s words, whom his master the king of the Assyrians sent to reproach the living God and to blaspheme with words which the Lord your God has heard. Take up a prayer for the remnant that remains.’

rationale: Sirach's birth-pain comparison recalls the crisis described in Isaiah: Hezekiah mourns and his messengers speak of a woman whose labor has come but who lacks strength to give birth.
source_text: Then their hearts and hands were shaken, and they suffered pangs like women giving birth.

target_units.text: When King Hezekiah heard, he tore his garments, wrapped himself in sackcloth, and went up to the Lord’s house.
He sent Eliakim the steward, Somnas the scribe, and the elders of the priests, wrapped in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah son of Amos.
They said to him, “Thus says Hezekiah: Today is a day of distress, reproach, reproof, and wrath, for labor has come upon the woman giving birth, but she has no strength to give birth.

May the Lord your God hear Rapsakes’ words, which the king of the Assyrians sent to reproach the living God and to reproach words that the Lord your God has heard. You shall plead with the Lord your God for those who remain.”

rationale: Sirach recalls prayer, God's hearing, and deliverance associated with Isaiah. Chronicles explicitly joins Hezekiah and Isaiah in prayer to heaven, then recounts the Lord's intervention and Jerusalem's deliverance from Sennacherib.
source_text: They called upon the merciful Lord, spreading their hands toward Him. The Holy One quickly heard them from heaven and redeemed them by Isaiah’s hand.

target_units.text: King Hezekiah and Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet prayed about these things and cried out to heaven.

The Lord sent an angel, and he wiped out every mighty warrior, ruler, and commander in the camp of the king of Assyria. The king returned to his land with shame of face. He entered the house of his god, and some who had come from his own body struck him down with the sword.
The Lord saved Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem from the hand of Sennacherib king of Assyria and from everyone’s hand, and He gave them rest all around.

rationale: Sirach says God heard the threatened people's petition. Kings records Hezekiah's plea for deliverance and Isaiah's message that the Lord has heard his prayer concerning Sennacherib.
source_text: They called upon the merciful Lord, spreading their hands toward Him. The Holy One quickly heard them from heaven and redeemed them by Isaiah’s hand.

target_units.text: Hezekiah took the letters from the messengers’ hand and read them. He went up to the Lord’s house, and Hezekiah unfolded them before the Lord.
He said, ‘Lord, Israel’s God, seated upon the cherubim, Thou alone art God among all the kingdoms of the earth. Thou madest heaven and earth.
Incline Thine ear, Lord, and hear. Open Thine eyes, Lord, and see. Hear Sennacherib’s words, which he sent to reproach the living God.
For truly, Lord, the kings of the Assyrians have devastated the nations
and put their gods into the fire, for they are not gods but the work of human hands, wood and stones; so they destroyed them.
Now, Lord our God, save us from his hand, and all the kingdoms of the earth will know that Thou art the Lord, God alone.’
Isaiah son of Amos sent to Hezekiah: ‘Thus says the Lord, the God of hosts, Israel’s God: What you did pray to Me concerning Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, I have heard.

rationale: Sirach credits an angel with striking the Assyrian camp. Kings narrates the Lord's angel striking that camp by night and the discovery of its dead in the morning.
source_text: He struck the Assyrians’ camp, and His angel destroyed them.

target_units.text: By night the Lord’s angel went out and struck one hundred eighty-five thousand in the Assyrians’ camp. When they rose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead bodies.

rationale: Sirach's destruction of the Assyrian camp through an angel has a parallel account in Isaiah, which names the angel of the Lord, the Assyrian camp, and the bodies discovered the following morning.
source_text: He struck the Assyrians’ camp, and His angel destroyed them.

target_units.text: An angel of the Lord went out and killed one hundred eighty-five thousand from the Assyrians’ camp. On rising early in the morning, they found all the bodies dead.

rationale: Sirach commends Hezekiah for following David's ways. Kings identifies Hezekiah's accession and expressly assesses his conduct by everything his father David had done.
source_text: For Hezekiah did what was pleasing to the Lord and stood strong in the ways of his father David, which Isaiah the prophet commanded, great and faithful in his vision.

target_units.text: In the third year of Hoshea son of Ela, king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz, king of Judah, became king.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Abou daughter of Zechariah.
He did what was right in the Lord’s eyes, in accordance with everything his father David had done.

rationale: Sirach joins the backward movement of the sun with the extension of the king's life. Kings promises Hezekiah fifteen additional years and narrates Isaiah's prayer and the shadow's return ten steps as the healing sign.
source_text: In his days the sun went backward, and He added life to the king.

target_units.text: Isaiah was in the middle courtyard when the Lord’s word came to him:

‘Return and tell Hezekiah, leader of My people: Thus says the Lord, the God of your father David: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears. Behold, I shall heal you; on the third day you shall go up to the Lord’s house,
and I shall add fifteen years to your days. I shall save you and this city from the hand of the king of the Assyrians, and shield this city for My own sake and for the sake of David My servant.’
He said, ‘Let them take a cake of figs and place it on the ulcer, and he will recover.’
Hezekiah said to Isaiah, ‘What is the sign that the Lord will heal me and I shall go up to the Lord’s house on the third day?’
Isaiah said, ‘This is the sign from the Lord that the Lord will do the word He has spoken: The shadow will advance ten steps, if it returns ten steps.’
Hezekiah said, ‘It is easy for the shadow to incline ten steps. No, let the shadow return ten steps backward.’
Isaiah the prophet cried to the Lord, and the shadow returned backward ten steps on the stairway.

rationale: Sirach's recollection of the reversed sun and prolonged life corresponds to Isaiah's account, where fifteen years are added to Hezekiah and the sun goes back up the ten steps as the promised sign.
source_text: In his days the sun went backward, and He added life to the king.

target_units.text: The Lord’s word came to Isaiah, saying,
“Go and tell Hezekiah: Thus says the Lord, God of David your father: I heard the voice of your prayer and saw your tears. Behold, I am adding fifteen years to your time.
I will save you from the king of the Assyrians’ hand, and I will shield this city.
This is your sign from the Lord that God will do this thing:”
“As for the shadow of the steps the sun descended—the ten steps of your father’s house—I will turn the sun back ten steps.” The sun went up the ten steps which the shadow had descended.

rationale: Sirach praises Isaiah's great spirit and comfort for Zion's mourners. Isaiah presents the Lord's spirit upon the commissioned speaker and explicitly promises comfort and transformed mourning for Zion.
source_text: With a great spirit he saw the last things and comforted those mourning in Zion.

target_units.text: The Lord’s spirit is upon me, because He anointed me. He sent me to bring good news to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind,
to announce the Lord’s acceptable year and a day of recompense, to comfort all who mourn,

so that Zion’s mourners may receive glory instead of ashes, an ointment of joy for those who mourn, a robe of glory instead of a spirit of despondency. They will be called Generations of Righteousness, the Lord’s planting, for glory.

rationale: Sirach recalls Isaiah comforting Zion's mourners. Isaiah's repeated call to comfort God's people is directed to Jerusalem, whose humiliation is fulfilled and whose sin is loosed.
source_text: With a great spirit he saw the last things and comforted those mourning in Zion.

target_units.text: Comfort, comfort My people, says God.
You priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem; comfort her. For her humiliation is fulfilled, her sin is loosed; for from the hand of the Lord she has received double for her sins.

rationale: Sirach describes Isaiah disclosing hidden things before they occur. Isaiah records the Lord announcing new things before they spring up; the foresight is presented in the target as God's declaration through the prophetic text.
source_text: He showed what would happen to the end of the age, and hidden things before they came to pass.

target_units.text: I am the Lord God; this is My name. I will not give My glory to another or My praiseworthy deeds to carved images.
Behold, the things from the beginning have arrived, and new things I will announce; before they spring up, they were disclosed to you.”

rationale: Sirach compares the memory of Josiah to finely prepared perfume. Ecclesiastes compares the value of a name with good oil, providing a related wisdom image in which personal reputation and good oil are brought together.
source_text: The remembrance of Josiah is like a blend of incense prepared by a perfumer’s skill. In every mouth it will be sweet as honey, and like music at a wine banquet.

target_units.text: A name is better than good oil, and the day of death than the day of one’s birth.

rationale: Sirach recalls Josiah turning the people back and removing abominations. Kings describes the renewed covenant, the people's participation, and his removal and destruction of objects associated with idolatrous worship.
source_text: He was rightly directed in bringing the people back, and he removed the abominations of lawlessness.

target_units.text: The king stood beside the pillar and made a covenant before the Lord: to follow the Lord and keep His commandments, testimonies, and ordinances with the whole heart and whole soul, upholding the words of this covenant, the things written in this book. All the people stood in the covenant.

The king commanded Chelkias the high priest, the priests of the second rank, and the doorpost guards to bring out of the Lord’s sanctuary all the vessels made for Baal, for the grove, and for all heaven’s host. He burned them outside Jerusalem in the sademoth of Kidron and took their dust to Bethel.

He put an end to the chomarim whom Judah’s kings had appointed, who burned incense at the high places and in Judah’s cities and the places around Jerusalem, and to those burning incense to Baal, the sun, the moon, the mazouroth, and all heaven’s host.

He brought the grove out of the Lord’s house, outside Jerusalem to the Kidron torrent. He burned it in the Kidron torrent, reduced it to dust, and threw its dust into the grave of the sons of the people.

rationale: Sirach's removal of abominations under Josiah corresponds to Chronicles' account of his seeking the Lord and cleansing Judah, Jerusalem, and other cities by destroying altars and sacred objects.
source_text: He was rightly directed in bringing the people back, and he removed the abominations of lawlessness.

target_units.text: In the eighth year of his reign, while still a boy, he began to seek the Lord, the God of his father David. In the twelfth year of his reign he began to cleanse Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, sacred groves, and cast objects.

He pulled down before him the altars of the Baals and the high places upon them. He cut down the sacred groves, shattered and pulverized the carved and cast objects, and scattered them over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them.
He burned priests’ bones upon the altars and cleansed Judah and Jerusalem.
And in the cities of Ephraim, Manasseh, Simeon, and Naphtali, and in their surrounding places,
he pulled down the sacred groves and altars, cut the idols into fine pieces, and cut down all the high places throughout the land of Israel. Then he returned to Jerusalem.

rationale: Sirach praises Josiah's directed heart and strengthening of godliness. Kings similarly singles him out for returning to the Lord with his whole heart, soul, and strength according to Moses' law.
source_text: He directed his heart toward the Lord; in days of lawless people he strengthened godliness.

target_units.text: Before him there was no king like him who returned to the Lord with his whole heart, his whole soul, and all his strength, according to all Moses’ law; and after him none like him arose.

rationale: Sirach connects Josiah's heart toward God with the people's godliness. Chronicles records his whole-hearted covenant, the people's renewed commitment, and his making those present serve the Lord throughout his days.
source_text: He directed his heart toward the Lord; in days of lawless people he strengthened godliness.

target_units.text: The king stood by the pillar and established a covenant before the Lord: to walk before the Lord and keep His commandments, testimonies, and ordinances with the whole heart and the whole soul—the words of the covenant written in this book.
He made everyone found in Jerusalem and Benjamin stand. The inhabitants of Jerusalem made a covenant in the house of the Lord, the God of their fathers.

Josiah removed all the abominations from all the land belonging to the sons of Israel and made everyone present in Jerusalem and Israel serve the Lord their God throughout his days. He did not turn aside from following the Lord, the God of his fathers.

rationale: Sirach links Judah's royal downfall with abandonment of the law. Chronicles gives the particular final-reign example of Zedekiah's refusal to return to God, the people's breaches of faith, and their rejection of prophetic messages until wrath came.
source_text: Except for David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, they all committed offenses. For they abandoned the law of the Most High; the kings of Judah came to an end.

target_units.text: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.
He did what was evil before the Lord his God. He felt no shame before Jeremiah the prophet, and at what came from the Lord’s mouth,
in breaking his obligations to King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God. He hardened his neck and strengthened his heart so as not to return to the Lord God of Israel.
All the distinguished men of Judah, the priests, and the people of the land multiplied breaches of faith in the nations’ abominations and defiled the Lord’s house in Jerusalem.
The Lord, the God of their fathers, sent through prophets, rising early and sending His messengers, because He spared His people and His sanctuary.
They kept sneering at His messengers, treating His words as nothing, and mocking His prophets, until the Lord’s anger rose among His people, until there was no healing.

rationale: Sirach describes Judah's strength and glory passing to foreigners. Chronicles recounts defeat by the Chaldean king, transfer of temple and royal treasures to Babylon, and the survivors' servitude there.
source_text: For they gave their horn to others and their glory to a foreign nation.

target_units.text: He brought against them a king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of his sanctuary and did not spare Zedekiah. They had no mercy on their virgins and carried away their elders. He handed everything into their hands.
All the vessels of God’s house, great and small, the treasures, and all the treasures of the king and the magnates—he brought everything into Babylon.
He burned the Lord’s house, demolished Jerusalem’s wall, and burned its citadels with fire, consigning every beautiful article to destruction.
He deported the survivors to Babylon, and they became slaves to him and his sons until the kingdom of the Medes,

rationale: Sirach recalls the city of the sanctuary being burned and its streets made desolate. Kings records the burning of the Lord's house, the king's house, and Jerusalem's houses, followed by removal of the remaining people.
source_text: They burned the chosen city of the sanctuary and made its streets desolate,

target_units.text: In the fifth month, on the seventh of the month, in the nineteenth year of Nabouchodonosor king of Babylon, Nabouzardan, the chief cook who stood before the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.
He set fire to the Lord’s house, the king’s house, and all Jerusalem’s houses; every house was set ablaze by
the chief cook.
Nabouzardan, the chief cook, removed the rest of the people left in the city, those who had gone over to the king of Babylon, and the remaining support.

rationale: Sirach's burning and desolation of Jerusalem correspond to Chronicles' destruction of the Lord's house, city wall, and citadels, followed by deportation of the survivors.
source_text: They burned the chosen city of the sanctuary and made its streets desolate,

target_units.text: He burned the Lord’s house, demolished Jerusalem’s wall, and burned its citadels with fire, consigning every beautiful article to destruction.
He deported the survivors to Babylon, and they became slaves to him and his sons until the kingdom of the Medes,

rationale: Sirach recalls Jeremiah's consecration in the womb and commission to destroy, build, and plant. Jeremiah's opening call explicitly places consecration before birth and appoints him to uproot, demolish, destroy, build, and plant.
source_text: by Jeremiah’s hand. For they mistreated him, though he was sanctified in the womb as a prophet to uproot, afflict, and destroy, and likewise to build and plant.

target_units.text: The Lord’s word came to me, saying,
Before I formed you in the belly, I know you; before you came out of the womb, I have consecrated you. I have appointed you a prophet to nations.
I said, O Master Lord! Behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am young.
The Lord said to me, Do not say, I am young, because you will go to everyone to whom I send you, and you will speak according to everything I command you.
Do not fear them, because I am with you to rescue you, says the Lord.
The Lord stretched out His hand toward me and touched my mouth. The Lord said to me, Behold, I have put My words into your mouth.
Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, demolish, destroy, build and plant.

rationale: Sirach praises Ezekiel's vision of glory. Ezekiel describes the throne-like form, its radiance, and the rainbow-like brightness, explicitly identifying this as the appearance of the likeness of the Lord's glory.
source_text: Ezekiel saw a vision of glory, which He showed him upon a chariot of cherubim.

target_units.text: Like the appearance of a sapphire stone was the likeness of a throne upon it; and above the likeness of the throne was a likeness like the form of a human being.

I saw something like the sight of electrum from the appearance of a waist upward; and from the appearance of a waist down below I saw something like the appearance of fire, with its brightness all around.

Like the appearance of a bow when it is in the cloud on a rainy day, so was the arrangement of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of the Lord’s glory. I saw it, and I fall upon my face, and I heard the voice of One speaking.

rationale: Sirach associates Ezekiel's glorious vision with the cherubim's chariot. Ezekiel describes the cherubim rising with wheels, the Lord's glory mounting them, and his recognition that these are the creatures seen at the river Chebar.
source_text: Ezekiel saw a vision of glory, which He showed him upon a chariot of cherubim.

target_units.text: The cherubim lifted themselves. This was the living creature I had seen at the river Chebar.
When the cherubim went, the wheels went beside them. When the cherubim raised their wings to rise from the earth, their wheels did not turn.
When they stood, these stood; when they rose, these rose with them, because a spirit of life was in them.
The Lord’s glory went out from the house and mounted upon the cherubim,

and the cherubim lifted their wings and rose from the earth before me as they went out, with the wheels beside them. They stood at the entrance of the opposite gate of the Lord’s house, and the glory of the God of Israel was above them.
This is the living creature I had seen beneath the God of Israel at the river Chebar, and I knew that it was cherubim.

rationale: Sirach speaks of God remembering enemies in a rainstorm. Ezekiel's oracle against Gog describes divine judgment through flooding rain and hailstones. The supported connection is this specific storm-judgment image; the passage does not establish that Sirach is identifying this particular oracle.
source_text: For He remembered the enemies in a rainstorm, and remembered to do good to those who make their ways straight.

target_units.text: I will judge him with death, blood, flooding rain and hailstones. I will rain fire and sulfur upon him, all those with him and the many nations with him.
I will be magnified, sanctified, glorified and made known before many nations, and they will know that I am the Lord.’”

rationale: Sirach honors the twelve prophets for comforting Jacob and sustaining hope of redemption. Zechariah supplies a particular example: the Lord answers with comforting words and promises compassion, rebuilding, and renewed mercy for Jerusalem and Zion.
source_text: May the bones of the twelve prophets flourish again from their place! For they comforted Jacob and redeemed them with the faithfulness of hope.

target_units.text: The Lord Almighty answered the angel speaking within me with good words and comforting speeches.
The angel speaking within me said to me, “Cry out: Thus says the Lord Almighty: I have been jealous for Jerusalem and Zion with great jealousy,
and I am angry with great anger at the nations joining in assault, because I was a little angry, but they joined in attacking to bring evils.
Therefore thus says the Lord: I will return to Jerusalem in compassion, and My house will be rebuilt in her, says the Lord Almighty, and a measure will again be extended over Jerusalem.”
The angel speaking within me said to me, “Cry out: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Cities will again overflow with good things; the Lord will again have mercy on Zion and again choose Jerusalem.”

rationale: Sirach prays that the twelve prophets' bones flourish from their place. The earlier praise of the judges likewise asks that their bones flourish from their place, repeating the memorial prayer for another group of Israel's honored ancestors.
source_text: May the bones of the twelve prophets flourish again from their place! For they comforted Jacob and redeemed them with the faithfulness of hope.

target_units.text: May their bones flourish again from their place, and may their name pass onward to their honored sons.

rationale: Sirach compares Zerubbabel to a signet on the right hand. Haggai's promise names Zerubbabel, calls him God's chosen servant, and says God will make him like a signet; Haggai does not specify the hand.
source_text: How shall we magnify Zerubbabel? He too was like a seal upon the right hand.

target_units.text: On that day, says the Lord Almighty, I will take you, Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, My servant, says the Lord, and make you like a signet, for I have chosen you, says the Lord Almighty.”

rationale: Sirach credits Joshua son of Jozadak and Zerubbabel with rebuilding the Lord's house. Ezra names the corresponding leaders as Iesous son of Iosedek and Zorobabel son of Salathiel and records their beginning to rebuild God's house with prophetic assistance.
source_text: So was Joshua son of Jozadak. In their days they built a house and raised up a holy sanctuary for the Lord, prepared for everlasting glory.

target_units.text: Haggai the prophet and Zacharias son of Addo prophesied a prophecy over the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel, over them.
Then Zorobabel son of Salathiel and Iesous son of Iosedek arose and began building the house of God in Jerusalem. God’s prophets were with them, helping them.

rationale: Sirach remembers Nehemiah for restoring the fallen walls. Nehemiah records the wall's completion and the surrounding nations' recognition that God brought the work to completion.
source_text: Great also is the remembrance of Nehemiah, who raised our fallen walls, set up gates and bars, and rebuilt our home sites.

target_units.text: The wall was completed on the twenty-fifth of Eloul, in fifty-two days.
When all our enemies heard, all the nations around us became afraid. Great fear fell upon them before their eyes, and they knew that it was by our God that this work had been brought to completion.

rationale: Sirach credits Nehemiah with restored walls and gates. Nehemiah records the built wall, the setting up of doors, and arrangements to close and guard them. This supports the wall and gate details; the adjacent verse 7:4 still says that houses had not been built.
source_text: Great also is the remembrance of Nehemiah, who raised our fallen walls, set up gates and bars, and rebuilt our home sites.

target_units.text: When the wall had been built, I set up the doors, and the gatekeepers, singers and Levites were appointed.
I gave orders to my brother Anania and to Anania, ruler of the bira in Jerusalem, for he was a truthful man and feared God more than many,

and I said to them, “The gates of Jerusalem shall not be opened until the sun is up. While they are still keeping watch, let the doors be closed and wedged fast. Appoint advance guards from those living in Jerusalem, each at his guard post and each opposite his house.”

rationale: Sirach distinguishes Enoch by his being taken from the earth. Genesis says that Enoch pleased God and was not found because God transferred him.
source_text: No one was created on earth like Enoch, for he was taken up from the earth.

target_units.text: And Enoch lived one hundred and sixty-five years, and begot Methuselah.
And Enoch pleased God for two hundred years after he begot Methuselah, and begot sons and daughters.
And all the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years.
And Enoch pleased God, and was not found, for God transferred him.

rationale: Sirach praises Enoch's exceptional removal from the earth. Hebrews explicitly recalls Enoch being taken away so as not to see death and connects that removal with his testimony of pleasing God.
source_text: No one was created on earth like Enoch, for he was taken up from the earth.

target_units.text: By faith Enoch was taken away so as not to see death, and he was not found, because God took him away. For before his taking away he had received testimony that he had pleased God.

rationale: Sirach says that care was taken of Joseph's bones. Genesis records Joseph's oath requiring his bones to be carried from Egypt at God's visitation, followed by his burial preparations and placement in a coffin.
source_text: Nor was a man born like Joseph, a leader of his brothers, a support for the people; and his bones were cared for.

target_units.text: And Joseph spoke to his brothers, saying, “I am dying; but God shall surely visit you, and bring you up from this land to the land which God swore to our fathers Abraham and Isaac and Jacob.”
And Joseph made the sons of Israel swear, saying, “In the visitation with which God shall visit you, you shall carry up my bones from here with you.”
And Joseph died, being a hundred and ten years old; and they performed his burial rites, and laid him in a coffin in Egypt.

rationale: Sirach remembers the care of Joseph's bones. Exodus records the carrying out of his oath when Moses takes those bones on Israel's departure from Egypt.
source_text: Nor was a man born like Joseph, a leader of his brothers, a support for the people; and his bones were cared for.

target_units.text: Moses took Joseph’s bones with him, for Joseph had made the sons of Israel swear an oath, saying, “The Lord will surely visit you, and you shall carry my bones up from here with you.”

rationale: Sirach's remembrance of Joseph's bones has a further narrative counterpart in Joshua, which records their transport from Egypt and burial in Joseph's inherited portion at Shechem.
source_text: Nor was a man born like Joseph, a leader of his brothers, a support for the people; and his bones were cared for.

target_units.text: The sons of Israel brought Joseph’s bones up from Egypt and buried them at Shechem in the portion of the field that Jacob acquired from the Amorites living at Shechem for one hundred ewe lambs; he gave it to Joseph as a portion.

rationale: Sirach places Adam above the living creatures in his account of ancestral honor. Genesis gives humankind God's image and authority over fish, birds, cattle, the earth, and creeping things, supplying the corresponding distinction within creation.
source_text: Shem and Seth were glorified among people, and Adam above every living creature in creation.

target_units.text: And God said, “Let Us make man in Our image and likeness; and let them rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the cattle, all the earth, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.”
And God made man; in the image of God He made him; male and female He made them.

And God blessed them, saying, “Grow and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it. Rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, all the cattle, all the earth, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.”

rationale: Sirach admires Simon as he emerges from the house of the veil. Leviticus describes the priest's service within the veil and excludes others until he comes out, supplying a parallel pattern of restricted priestly entry and exit without identifying Simon's particular festival.
source_text: How glorious he was with the people surrounding him, when he came out from the house of the veil!

target_units.text: And he shall slaughter the male young goat for the people’s sin offering before the Lord and bring some of its blood within the veil. He shall do with its blood as he did with the calf’s blood, sprinkling its blood on the propitiatory cover, before the propitiatory cover,

and make atonement for the holy place from the sons of Israel’s uncleannesses and their wrongdoings, concerning all their sins. He shall do the same for the Tent of Testimony established among them amid their uncleanness.

And no one shall be in the Tent of Testimony when he enters to make atonement in the holy place until he comes out. He shall make atonement for himself, his house, and the whole congregation of the sons of Israel.

rationale: Sirach compares Simon's splendor to the full moon. The Song compares its praised woman to dawn and the beautiful moon; the shared celestial image describes beauty, while the persons and settings remain different.
source_text: He was like the morning star among clouds, like the full moon in its days,

target_units.text: My dove, my perfect one, is the only one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of the woman who bore her. Daughters saw her and will call her blessed; queens and concubines will praise her.
Who is this looking out like dawn, beautiful like the moon, chosen like the sun, a terror like troops drawn up?

rationale: Sirach compares Simon's splendor to a rainbow gleaming in glorious clouds. Ezekiel uses the rainbow in a rainy cloud to describe the brightness of the Lord's glory. The comparison concerns the luminous image, without equating the priest with God.
source_text: like the sun shining upon the sanctuary of the Most High, and like the rainbow gleaming in clouds of glory,

target_units.text: Like the appearance of a bow when it is in the cloud on a rainy day, so was the arrangement of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of the Lord’s glory. I saw it, and I fall upon my face, and I heard the voice of One speaking.

rationale: Sirach portrays Simon through lilies near water and a shoot of Lebanon. Hosea describes restored Israel receiving dew, blossoming like a lily, and putting down roots like Lebanon; both use flourishing plants and Lebanon to portray renewed beauty.
source_text: like a rose blossom in the days of new growth, like lilies beside an outflow of water, like a shoot of Lebanon in summer days,

target_units.text: I will be like dew to Israel; he will blossom like a lily and put down his roots like Lebanon.
His branches will spread, and he will be like an olive tree laden with fruit; his fragrance will be like Lebanon.

rationale: Sirach likens Simon's splendor to fire and frankincense upon a firepan. Leviticus describes the priest taking a firepan of burning coals and putting incense on the fire before the Lord, providing the particular ritual image used in the simile.
source_text: like fire and frankincense upon a firepan, like a vessel of beaten gold adorned with every costly stone,

target_units.text: And he shall take the firepan full of burning coals from the altar opposite the Lord, fill his hands with finely compounded incense, and bring them within the veil,
and put the incense on the fire before the Lord. The vapour of incense shall cover the propitiatory cover above the testimonies, and he shall not die.

rationale: Sirach compares Simon to a fruitful olive and a towering cypress. Wisdom's earlier self-description likewise uses the cypress and stately olive; the botanical images recur with different subjects.
source_text: like an olive tree flourishing with fruit, and like a cypress rising into the clouds.

target_units.text: I rose high like a cedar in Lebanon, like a cypress in the mountains of Hermon.
I rose high like a palm in En-gedi, like rose plants in Jericho, like a stately olive in the plain; I rose high like a plane tree.

rationale: Sirach describes Simon's robe of glory and priestly splendor. Exodus orders Aaron's holy robe for honor and glory and enumerates garments made for priestly service, supplying the corresponding purpose of glorious priestly dress.
source_text: When he took up the robe of glory and clothed himself with the fullness of splendor, as he ascended the holy altar he glorified the sanctuary’s enclosure.

target_units.text: You shall make a holy robe for Aaron your brother, for honour and glory.
Speak to everyone skilled in understanding whom I have filled with a spirit of perception. They shall make Aaron’s holy robe for the sanctuary, in which he shall serve Me as priest.

These are the robes they shall make: a breastpiece, a shoulder-piece, a full-length robe, a tasselled tunic, a turban, and a sash. They shall make holy robes for Aaron and his sons to serve Me as priests.

rationale: Sirach compares the priests surrounding the altar to Lebanon's cedars and palm trunks. The Psalm compares righteous people to palms and Lebanon's cedars and places their flourishing in the Lord's house and courts, joining the same trees with worship's setting.
source_text: When he received portions from the priests’ hands, standing himself beside the altar hearth, a crown of brothers surrounded him, like a growth of cedars in Lebanon; they encircled him like palm trunks,

target_units.text: A righteous person will blossom like a palm tree; like the cedar in Lebanon he will multiply.
Planted in the Lord’s house, they will blossom in the courts of our God.

rationale: Sirach depicts Aaron's sons with offerings before Israel's assembly. Leviticus places the congregation before the Lord and describes Aaron at the altar with his sons bringing him the sacrificial blood.
source_text: all the sons of Aaron in their glory, with the Lord’s offering in their hands before the whole assembly of Israel.

target_units.text: And they brought what Moses commanded opposite the Tent of Testimony, and the whole congregation drew near and stood before the Lord.
And Moses said: Do this thing which the Lord said, and the glory of the Lord shall appear among you.

And Moses said unto Aaron: Draw near unto the altar, and prepare your offering for sin and your whole burnt offering, and make atonement for yourself and your house; and prepare the gifts of the people, and make atonement for them, as the Lord commanded Moses.
And Aaron drew near unto the altar and slaughtered the calf for the sin offering.
And Aaron’s sons brought the blood to him. He dipped his finger in the blood, put it on the altar’s horns, and poured the blood at the altar’s base.

rationale: Sirach describes the high priest completing his altar ministry and offering. Chronicles describes the offering on the altar and the accompanying assembly's worship, singing, and trumpets continuing until the burnt offering is finished.
source_text: As he completed his ministry at the altars, adorning the offering of the Most High Almighty,

target_units.text: Hezekiah ordered the burnt offering to be offered on the altar. When they began offering the burnt offering, they began singing to the Lord, and the trumpets accompanied the instruments of David king of Israel.
The whole assembly worshiped, the psalm singers sang, and the trumpets sounded until the burnt offering was finished.

rationale: Sirach recounts the pouring of a drink offering before the Most High. Numbers prescribes pouring out a drink offering of strong drink to the Lord in the holy place; it supports the libation practice without specifying Sirach's altar-foundation detail.
source_text: he stretched his hand over the libation vessel and poured a drink offering from the blood of the grape. He poured it at the altar’s foundations, a pleasing fragrance to the Most High, King of all.

target_units.text: And its drink offering shall be a fourth of a hin for each lamb; in the holy place you shall pour out a drink offering of strong drink unto the Lord.

rationale: Sirach calls the libation wine the blood of the grape. Deuteronomy likewise names wine as the blood of the grape in its account of provision, sharing the particular image although the target describes drinking rather than a libation.
source_text: he stretched his hand over the libation vessel and poured a drink offering from the blood of the grape. He poured it at the altar’s foundations, a pleasing fragrance to the Most High, King of all.

target_units.text: butter of cattle and milk of sheep, with the fat of lambs and rams, young bulls and goats, with the fat of the kernels of wheat; and they drank wine, the blood of the grape.

rationale: Sirach describes Aaron's sons sounding trumpets as a remembrance before the Most High. Numbers assigns the trumpets to Aaron's priestly sons and expressly makes their sounding over offerings a remembrance before God.
source_text: Then the sons of Aaron cried out and sounded their hammered trumpets. They made a great sound heard as a remembrance before the Most High.

target_units.text: And Aaron’s sons, the priests, shall blow the trumpets. This shall be an everlasting statute for you throughout your generations.

But if you go out to war in your land against the adversaries who resist you, you shall give a signal with the trumpets; and you shall be remembered before the Lord, and shall be delivered from your enemies.

And in the days of your gladness, and at your feasts, and at your new moons, you shall blow the trumpets over your whole burnt offerings and over your sacrifices of deliverance; and it shall be a remembrance for you before your God. I am the Lord your God.

rationale: Sirach's assembled people fall facedown to worship the Lord during the temple service. Chronicles recounts Israel's collective prostration on the pavement in response to the Lord's glory at the temple dedication; these are corresponding acts in different ceremonies.
source_text: Then all the people together hurried and fell facedown upon the earth to worship their Lord, the Almighty God Most High.

target_units.text: When Solomon finished praying, fire came down from heaven and consumed the whole burnt offerings and sacrifices, and the Lord’s glory filled the house.
The priests could not enter the Lord’s house at that time, because the Lord’s glory had filled the house.

All Israel’s sons saw the fire descending and the Lord’s glory upon the house. They fell face down to the earth upon the stone pavement, worshiped, and praised the Lord: “For it is good, for His mercy endures for ever.”

rationale: Sirach praises the psalm singers' voices and the great sound of their melody. Chronicles describes the assembled Levitical singers and instruments joining in one voice to give thanks and praise at the sanctuary.
source_text: The psalm singers praised with their voices; amid a very great sound the melody grew sweet.

target_units.text: and all the Levitical singers belonging to the sons of Asaph, to Heman, and to Idithoun, and their sons and their brethren, clothed in fine-linen robes, with cymbals, nablai, and kinyrai, stood opposite the altar, and with them were a hundred and twenty priests sounding trumpets,

there was one voice in trumpeting, singing psalms, and shouting, to give thanks and praise to the Lord. When they raised their voice with trumpets, cymbals, and musical instruments, they said, “Give thanks to the Lord, for it is good, for His mercy endures for ever.” The house was filled with a cloud of the Lord’s glory.

rationale: Sirach describes the people praying while the Lord's ceremony is completed. Luke likewise places the congregation's prayer alongside priestly service, with the multitude praying outside while the priest burns incense inside.
source_text: The people entreated the Lord Most High in prayer before the Merciful One, until the Lord’s ceremony was completed and they finished His service.

target_units.text: While he was serving as priest before God in the order of his division,
according to the priesthood’s custom, he was chosen by lot to enter the Lord’s sanctuary and burn incense.
The whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense.

rationale: Sirach describes Simon coming down and raising his hands over Israel to bless them. Leviticus describes Aaron lifting his hands over the people, blessing them, and coming down after the offerings; the correspondence concerns the priestly gesture and blessing.
source_text: Then he came down and raised his hands over the whole assembly of the sons of Israel, to give the Lord’s blessing from his lips and to glory in His name.

target_units.text: And Aaron lifted his hands over the people and blessed them. He came down after preparing the offering for sin, the whole burnt offerings, and the deliverance offerings.
And Moses and Aaron entered the Tent of Testimony. They came out and blessed all the people, and the Lord’s glory appeared to all the people.

rationale: Sirach associates the priest's spoken blessing with the Lord's name. Numbers instructs Aaron and his sons to bless Israel, explicitly placing God's name upon them in this edition's verse 23, and gives the words of the blessing.
source_text: Then he came down and raised his hands over the whole assembly of the sons of Israel, to give the Lord’s blessing from his lips and to glory in His name.

target_units.text: Speak unto Aaron and unto his sons, saying: Thus you shall bless the sons of Israel, saying unto them (and they shall put My name upon the sons of Israel, and I, the Lord, will bless them):
The Lord bless you and keep you;
the Lord make His face shine upon you, and have mercy upon you;
the Lord lift up His face upon you, and give you peace.

rationale: Sirach depicts the people bowing to receive the blessing after priestly service. Leviticus joins the priests' blessing, the appearance of divine glory, and the congregation's falling on their faces; the latter response also follows the fire consuming the offering.
source_text: They bowed down a second time to receive the blessing from the Most High.

target_units.text: And Aaron lifted his hands over the people and blessed them. He came down after preparing the offering for sin, the whole burnt offerings, and the deliverance offerings.
And Moses and Aaron entered the Tent of Testimony. They came out and blessed all the people, and the Lord’s glory appeared to all the people.
And fire came out from the Lord and consumed what was on the altar, both the whole burnt offerings and the fat. All the people saw, were astonished, and fell on their faces.

rationale: Sirach calls for blessing the God who exalts human days from the womb. The Psalm acknowledges support from the womb and shelter from the mother's belly, and joins that lifelong dependence with continual praise.
source_text: And now bless the God of all, who does great things everywhere, who exalts our days from the womb and deals with us according to His mercy.

target_units.text: For Thou art my endurance, Lord; the Lord is my hope from my youth.
Upon Thee I was supported from the womb; from my mother’s belly Thou art the One who shelters me. My hymn is continually in Thee.

rationale: Sirach petitions God for gladness of heart and peace in Israel. Romans similarly prays that God fill its hearers with joy and peace in believing, within its own setting of hope shared by Jews and Gentiles.
source_text: May He give us gladness of heart, and may there be peace in Israel in our days, throughout the days of eternity.

target_units.text: And may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope in the power of the Holy Spirit.

rationale: Sirach prays that God's mercy be entrusted to His people and that He redeem them. The Psalm connects the Lord's mercy with abundant redemption and explicitly promises the redemption of Israel.
source_text: May He entrust His mercy to us, and in our days may He redeem us.

target_units.text: For with the Lord is mercy, and with Him is abundant redemption,
And He will redeem Israel from all its lawless deeds.

rationale: Sirach describes the author's wisdom pouring like rain from his heart. Deuteronomy asks that the speaker's utterance be awaited like rain and his words descend like dew, using rainfall imagery for beneficial teaching without identifying the two speakers.
source_text: Jesus son of Sirach Eleazar, the Jerusalemite, inscribed instruction in understanding and knowledge in this book; he poured wisdom like rain from his heart.

target_units.text: Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words of my mouth.
Let my utterance be awaited as the rain, and let my words descend as the dew, as a shower upon the grass, and as snow upon the herbage.
For I have called upon the name of the Lord; ascribe greatness unto our God.

rationale: Sirach promises wisdom to the reader who occupies himself with these teachings and places them on his heart. The Psalm connects meditation on God's law and testimonies with becoming wiser and gaining understanding.
source_text: Blessed is the one who will occupy himself with these things; by setting them upon his heart he will become wise.

target_units.text: Thirteen: Mēm. How I loved Thy law, Lord! It is my meditation all day.
Thou madest me wiser than my enemies in Thy commandment, for it is mine for ever.
I understood more than all who teach me, for Thy testimonies are my meditation.
I understood more than elders, for I sought Thy commandments.

rationale: Sirach says that one practicing the instruction has the Lord's light as his path. The Psalm calls God's word a lamp to the feet and a light to the paths, sharing the image of divine guidance illuminating one's course.
source_text: For if he does them, he will be strong for everything, because the Lord’s light is his path.

target_units.text: Fourteen: Noun. Thy word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.

rationale: Sirach addresses God as Lord and King and promises praise and thanksgiving to His name. The Psalm likewise addresses God as King and promises daily blessing and praise of His name.
source_text: I will give thanks to Thee, Lord and King, and praise Thee, God my Savior. I give thanks to Thy name,

target_units.text: A praise of David. I will exalt Thee, my God, my King, and bless Thy name for the age and for the age of the age.
Every day I will bless Thee and praise Thy name for the age and for the age of the age.

rationale: Sirach thanks God for rescue from a slanderous tongue and false lips. The Psalm recounts an answered cry in affliction and explicitly asks for rescue from unjust lips and a deceitful tongue.
source_text: because Thou didst become my shelter and helper. Thou didst redeem my body from destruction and from the snare of a slanderous tongue, from lips that work falsehood. Before those standing around, Thou didst become my helper and redeem me,

target_units.text: A song of the ascents. To the Lord, when I was afflicted, I cried, and He heard me.
Lord, rescue my soul from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue.

rationale: Sirach recalls gnashing teeth and the threat of being devoured by those seeking his life. The Psalm describes enemies gnashing their teeth and asks that the speaker's life be restored from their wickedness and from lions.
source_text: according to the abundance of Thy mercy and Thy name, from gnashing teeth when I was ready to be devoured, from the hand of those seeking my life, from the many afflictions I had,

target_units.text: They tested me and mocked me with mockery; they gnashed their teeth at me.
Lord, when wilt Thou look upon this? Restore my soul from their wickedness, my only life from lions.

rationale: Sirach thanks God for rescue from surrounding fire. The Psalm recalls a community passing through fire and water before being brought to refreshment; it presents its ordeal as divine testing, while Sirach specifies a fire he did not kindle.
source_text: from the choking of a fire all around, and from the midst of a fire that I did not kindle,

target_units.text: For Thou didst test us, God; Thou didst try us by fire as silver is tried by fire.
Thou broughtest us into the trap; Thou didst place afflictions upon our back.
Thou madest human beings mount our heads; we passed through fire and water, and Thou broughtest us out to refreshment.

rationale: Sirach describes rescue from the belly of Hades. Jonah's prayer from the sea creature likewise speaks of crying from the belly of Hades and being heard by God, sharing this particular image of extremity.
source_text: from the depth of Hades’ belly, from an unclean tongue and a false word—

target_units.text: Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from the sea creature’s belly,
and said: “In my affliction I cried to the Lord my God, and He listened to me. From the belly of Hades Thou didst hear the voice of my cry.

rationale: Sirach recounts slander reaching a king and threatening his life. David likewise challenges Saul's acceptance of people's accusations, demonstrates his innocence, and says that Saul seeks to take his life; the parallel concerns the situation, without identifying Sirach's unnamed king as Saul.
source_text: slander to a king from an unjust tongue. My soul drew near to death, and my life was close to Hades below.

target_units.text: David rose behind him from the cave, and David called after Saul, saying, “Lord king!” Saul looked behind him, and David bent with his face to the ground and bowed to him.
David said to Saul, “Why do you listen to the people’s words, saying, ‘Behold, David seeks your soul’?

Behold, on this day your eyes have seen how the Lord handed you into my hand today in the cave. I was unwilling to kill you and spared you. I said, ‘I will not bring my hand against my lord, for this one is the Lord’s anointed.’

Behold, the flap of your double cloak is in my hand! I removed the flap and did not kill you. Know and see today that there is no evil in my hand, nor impiety or rejection. I have not sinned against you, yet you bind my soul to take it.
May the Lord judge between me and you, and may the Lord avenge me on you, but my hand shall not be against you.

rationale: Sirach describes being surrounded without any human helper. The Psalm joins approaching affliction with the explicit absence of anyone to help, turning that condition into an appeal for God's nearness.
source_text: They surrounded me on every side, and there was no helper. I looked for support from people, but there was none.

target_units.text: Do not stand away from me, for affliction is near, for there is no one to help.

rationale: Sirach remembers God's ancient mercy and rescue of those who wait for Him. The Psalm assures those who wait for God, addresses Him as Savior, and asks Him to remember His compassions and mercies from eternity.
source_text: I remembered Thy mercy, Lord, and Thy work from of old: Thou rescuest those who wait for Thee and savest them from the hand of enemies.

target_units.text: For indeed, all who wait for Thee will certainly not be put to shame; let all who act lawlessly without cause be ashamed.
Make Thy ways known to me, Lord, and teach me Thy paths.
Guide me into Thy truth and teach me, for Thou art God my Savior, and I waited for Thee the whole day.
Remember Thy compassions, Lord, and Thy mercies, for they are from eternity.
Do not remember the sins of my youth or my acts of ignorance; according to Thy mercy, remember me Thyself, for Thy kindness’ sake, Lord.

rationale: Sirach recalls pleading for deliverance from death. The Psalm describes death's pangs and Hades' dangers and gives the ensuing cry to the Lord to rescue the speaker's soul.
source_text: I lifted my supplication from the earth and pleaded for deliverance from death.

target_units.text: The pangs of death surrounded me; the dangers of Hades found me; I found affliction and pain.
And I called on the name of the Lord: “O Lord, rescue my soul!”

rationale: Sirach asks not to be abandoned in affliction when no help is available. The Psalm likewise asks the Lord not to abandon the speaker and to attend to his aid. This supports the petition, without interpreting Sirach's distinctive address, the Father of my Lord.
source_text: I called upon the Lord, the Father of my Lord, not to abandon me in days of affliction, in a time of arrogance when there was no help. I will praise Thy name continually and sing hymns with thanksgiving.

target_units.text: Do not abandon me, Lord; my God, do not depart from me.
Attend to my aid, Lord of my salvation.

rationale: Sirach's petition ends with the resolve to praise God's name continually. The Psalm likewise promises blessing at every time, continual praise in the mouth, and the shared exaltation of the Lord's name.
source_text: I called upon the Lord, the Father of my Lord, not to abandon me in days of affliction, in a time of arrogance when there was no help. I will praise Thy name continually and sing hymns with thanksgiving.

target_units.text: I will bless the Lord at every time; His praise is continually in my mouth.
My soul will be praised in the Lord; let the meek hear and rejoice.
Magnify the Lord with me; let us exalt His name together.

rationale: Sirach connects the hearing of his petition with rescue from destruction and an evil time. The Psalm similarly says that the Lord heard the poor man's cry and saved him from all his afflictions.
source_text: My petition was heard, for Thou didst save me from destruction and rescue me from an evil time.

target_units.text: This poor man cried out, and the Lord heard him; from all his afflictions He saved him.

rationale: Sirach responds to the rescue just recounted with thanksgiving and praise. The Psalm moves from mourning transformed into gladness to a promise of praise and everlasting thanks, supplying the corresponding response to deliverance.
source_text: Therefore I will give thanks to Thee and praise Thee and bless the Lord’s name.

target_units.text: Thou didst turn my lament into dancing for me; Thou didst tear open my sackcloth and gird me with gladness,
so that my glory may sing praise unto Thee, and I may certainly not be pierced with grief. Lord my God, I will thank Thee for ever.

rationale: Sirach remembers seeking wisdom in prayer while young. Solomon's prayer similarly describes him as a little child, asks for a discerning heart, and receives the Lord's gift of a wise heart; the accounts concern different petitioners.
source_text: While I was still young, before I wandered, I openly sought wisdom in my prayer.

target_units.text: Now, Lord my God, Thou hast placed Thy servant in place of my father David. I am a little child and do not know my going out or my coming in.
Thy servant is among Thy people whom Thou didst choose, a numerous people who cannot be numbered.
Give Thy servant a heart to hear and to judge Thy people in righteousness, discerning between good and evil; for who can judge this weighty people of Thine?”
It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this.
The Lord said to him, “Because you have asked this of Me and have not asked for many days for yourself, or wealth, or the lives of your enemies, but have asked for understanding to hear judgment,
behold, I have done according to your word. Behold, I have given you a discerning and wise heart, so that no one like you has been before you, and no one like you shall arise after you.

rationale: After recalling his youthful search, Sirach promises to seek wisdom until the end. The earlier instruction likewise spans a lifetime, beginning the choice of instruction in youth and continuing the finding of wisdom into gray-haired age.
source_text: Before the sanctuary I asked for her, and until the end I will seek her out.

target_units.text: Child, choose instruction from your youth, and until your hair is gray you will find wisdom.

rationale: Sirach describes his foot walking in uprightness as he traces wisdom's path. Proverbs joins instruction in wisdom with straight tracks, unhindered steps, and holding fast to discipline, sharing the portrayal of learning as a well-directed walk.
source_text: From her blossom, as from a ripening grape, my heart rejoiced in her. My foot stepped in uprightness; from my youth I traced her path.

target_units.text: for I teach you ways of wisdom and lead you onto straight tracks.
For if you walk, your steps will not be shut in, and if you run, you will not grow weary.
Take hold of my discipline; do not release it, but keep it for yourself for your life.

rationale: Sirach describes inclining his ear, receiving, and finding much instruction. Proverbs likewise connects receiving the commandment, the ear's obedience to wisdom, and the application of the heart with finding the knowledge of God.
source_text: I inclined my ear a little and received, and found much instruction for myself.

target_units.text: Son, if you receive an utterance of my commandment and hide it within yourself,
your ear will obey wisdom, and you will apply your heart to understanding; you will also apply it to admonishing your son.
for if you call upon wisdom and give your voice to understanding, and seek perception with a loud voice,
and if you seek it like silver and search it out like treasures,
then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God.

rationale: Sirach gives glory to the One who gives him wisdom. Proverbs explicitly identifies the Lord as the giver of wisdom and the source of knowledge and understanding.
source_text: I made progress in her; I will give glory to the One who gives me wisdom.

target_units.text: For the Lord gives wisdom, and from His presence come knowledge and understanding.

rationale: Sirach resolves to practice wisdom and declares that he will not be put to shame. The Psalm similarly wishes for ways directed to keeping God's ordinances and connects attention to the commandments with freedom from shame.
source_text: For I resolved to practice her and was zealous for the good, and I will never be put to shame.

target_units.text: If only my ways were directed to keep Thine ordinances!
Then I will certainly not be ashamed when I look upon all Thy commandments.

rationale: Sirach mourns his unwitting faults while seeking faithful practice of the law. The Psalm asks who can understand transgressions and requests cleansing of hidden faults, expressing the corresponding concern for sins beyond full awareness.
source_text: My soul has struggled for her, and I was exact in practicing the law. I spread my hands toward the height and mourned my soul’s unwitting faults.

target_units.text: Who will understand transgressions? Cleanse me of my hidden things.
And spare Thy servant from others; if they do not rule over me, then I will be blameless and cleansed from great sin.

rationale: Sirach directs his soul toward wisdom and describes finding her in purity. Wisdom of Solomon joins seeking God in simplicity of heart with the warning that wisdom does not enter an evil-devising soul or dwell in a body indebted to sin.
source_text: I directed my soul toward her and found her in purity. From the beginning I gained a heart together with her; therefore I will never be abandoned.

target_units.text: Love righteousness, you who judge the earth; think of the Lord in goodness, and seek Him in simplicity of heart.
For He is found by those who do not put Him to the test, and He makes Himself known to those who do not distrust Him.
For crooked reasonings separate from God, and power, when put to the test, exposes the foolish.
For wisdom will not enter a soul that devises evil, nor will she dwell in a body indebted to sin.
For a holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit and depart from senseless reasonings, and will be put to shame when injustice comes upon it.

rationale: Sirach's inward desire to seek wisdom results in acquiring a good possession. Proverbs likewise urges searching for wisdom like silver and treasure and describes the discovery of divine knowledge and the Lord's gift of wisdom.
source_text: My inward parts were stirred to seek her out; therefore I acquired a good possession.

target_units.text: for if you call upon wisdom and give your voice to understanding, and seek perception with a loud voice,
and if you seek it like silver and search it out like treasures,
then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God.
For the Lord gives wisdom, and from His presence come knowledge and understanding.

rationale: Sirach acknowledges a tongue given by the Lord and resolves to use it for praise. The Psalm likewise connects the Lord's opening of the lips with the mouth's announcement of His praise.
source_text: The Lord gave me a tongue as my reward, and with it I will praise Him.

target_units.text: Lord, Thou wilt open my lips, and my mouth will announce Thy praise.

rationale: Sirach invites the uninstructed to lodge in a house of instruction. Proverbs personifies Wisdom as building a house and summoning those lacking understanding to come, leave foolishness, and seek understanding.
source_text: Draw near to me, you who are uninstructed, and lodge in a house of instruction.

target_units.text: Wisdom built herself a house, and set seven pillars beneath it.
She slaughtered her own sacrificial animals, mixed her own wine in a mixing-bowl, and prepared her own table.
She sent her own servants, summoning with a lofty proclamation to the mixing-bowl, saying:
“Whoever is foolish, let him turn aside to me!” And to those lacking understanding she said:
“Come, eat of my loaves, and drink wine that I mixed for you.
Leave foolishness, and you will live; seek understanding, so that you may live, and set insight right in knowledge.”

rationale: Sirach addresses souls that thirst while lacking instruction. Isaiah likewise addresses the thirsty, invites them to freely provided nourishment, and connects listening with the soul's life and delight; the nourishment functions within an invitation to hear God.
source_text: Why do you say you are lacking in these things, while your souls thirst exceedingly?

target_units.text: You who thirst, go to the water; and you who have no silver, go and buy wine and rich food, and drink without silver or price.
Why do you pay a price of silver, and give your toil for what does not satisfy? Listen to Me, and you will eat good things, and your soul will delight in good things.
Listen with your ears, and follow My ways; listen to Me, and your soul will live amid good things. And I will make with you an everlasting covenant: the holy and sure blessings of David.

rationale: Sirach urges hearers to acquire instruction without silver. Isaiah similarly invites those without silver to buy without silver or price and to listen for the soul's life, joining the free-acquisition image with receptive hearing.
source_text: I opened my mouth and said, “Acquire for yourselves without silver.

target_units.text: You who thirst, go to the water; and you who have no silver, go and buy wine and rich food, and drink without silver or price.
Why do you pay a price of silver, and give your toil for what does not satisfy? Listen to Me, and you will eat good things, and your soul will delight in good things.
Listen with your ears, and follow My ways; listen to Me, and your soul will live amid good things. And I will make with you an everlasting covenant: the holy and sure blessings of David.

rationale: Sirach joins putting the neck under a yoke with receiving instruction. Jesus likewise invites hearers to take His yoke and learn from Him, coupling the teaching image with rest and a light burden; this is a comparison of the invitations, not an identification of their speakers.
source_text: “Put your neck beneath the yoke, and let your soul receive instruction. She is near at hand to be found.

target_units.text: Come to Me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest.
Take My yoke upon you, and learn from Me; for I am meek and lowly in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls.
For My yoke is easy, and My burden is light.”

rationale: Sirach's final invitation places the neck beneath wisdom's yoke. The earlier exhortation likewise places the neck in her collar, urges whole-soul pursuit, and promises the discovery of her rest.
source_text: “Put your neck beneath the yoke, and let your soul receive instruction. She is near at hand to be found.

target_units.text: Put your feet into her fetters and your neck into her collar.
Place your shoulder beneath her and carry her, and do not resent her bonds.
Approach her with all your soul, and keep her ways with your whole strength.
Trace her out and seek her, and she will become known to you; when you have gained hold of her, do not let her go.
For in the end you will find her rest, and she will turn to gladness for you.

rationale: Sirach contrasts the little labor of seeking wisdom with the much rest he found. Jesus addresses those laboring and burdened with a promise of rest and describes His burden as light. Both connect the teacher's invitation with rest, while describing its demands as little labor or a light burden.
source_text: “See with your own eyes that I labored a little and found much rest for myself.

target_units.text: Come to Me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest.
Take My yoke upon you, and learn from Me; for I am meek and lowly in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls.
For My yoke is easy, and My burden is light.”

rationale: Sirach urges costly participation in instruction using silver and gold as its value imagery. Proverbs places discipline and knowledge above silver and tested gold; the comparison concerns wisdom's worth and does not turn Sirach's image into a guarantee of financial profit.
source_text: “Take part in instruction at the cost of much silver, and acquire much gold through her.

target_units.text: Take discipline rather than silver, and knowledge above tested gold; choose discernment rather than pure gold.
For wisdom is better than costly stones, and nothing precious is worthy of her.

rationale: Sirach exhorts the soul to rejoice in God's mercy. The Psalm likewise promises exultation and rejoicing in divine mercy and grounds that response in rescue from humiliation and an enemy's grasp.
source_text: “May your soul rejoice in His mercy, and may you not be ashamed in His praise.

target_units.text: I will exult and rejoice in Thy mercy, because Thou didst look upon my humiliation; Thou didst save my soul from constraints
and didst not enclose me in an enemy’s hands; Thou didst set my feet in a spacious place.

rationale: Sirach urges work before the appointed time and trusts God to give the reward in His time. Galatians similarly joins doing good while opportunity remains with the assurance of reaping in the proper season if one does not give up.
source_text: “Do your work before the appointed time, and He will give you your reward in His time.”

target_units.text: Do not be deceived; God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.
For the one who sows into his own flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but the one who sows into the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.
And let us not grow weary in doing good, for in the proper season we will reap, if we do not give up.
So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, especially to those of the household of faith.
